Latest Update: The Best Cellular Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot.
  • Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot. For hunters on a budget, the SpyPoint Flex-M2 is the pick. Need maximum detection range, choose the Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0. For the sharpest images, the Stealth Cam Deceptor Max 3.0 leads the field.

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

According to recent reports, I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s. I remember walking laps around the local Walmart, waiting for the one-hour photo lab to process my prints. Most of the time, it was 24 images of a branch that the wind blew back and forth. Occasionally, I’d get a deer—sometimes even a good buck.

Trail cams have come a long way since, and, of course, cellular trail cameras dominate the scene today. If you want to learn all you can about the critters you hunt without setting foot in the woods other than to change batteries or move a camera or two, cellular trail cameras are the way to go. But which cell cams?

Recent findings suggest that to help you figure out which models are right for you, I spent two months running and testing the latest new-for-2026 cell cams in my backyard and on a nearby 700-acre whitetail property in Colorado. Testing conditions were difficult. Every camera was exposed to heavy wind, a 60-day average high temperature of 95.7 degrees, rain, and hail that damaged roofs. The good news: There were no flops. I would have no reservations running any of the new cellular cams below anywhere in the country. That remarked, some proved better than others depending on what your value most. So, let’s dive in. Here are the best cellular trail cameras of 2026.

Industry observers note that one complaint I’ve always had about cellular trail cameras is the antennas, as they are always breaking off in backpacks or the back seat of my truck. Mother Nature has her way with them, dropping dead branches and crushing skinny, side-mounted antennas. I’ve even broken a couple by catching the antenna in my pant leg while walking to a stand in the dark.

Sources indicate that browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV features an innovative, wide, blade-style antenna located in the center of the trail camera. It’s extra-sturdy and folds back and locks into the back of the main camera housing for easy, secure transport. The high-gain antenna also grabbed the most available network more quickly than any other camera in this year’s test.

The MAX HD DV uses the same straightforward interface on the camera’s lower housing behind the lock-and-latch door that Browning users are used to and appreciate. The 1.5-inch LED screen is bright, and the soft-push buttons don’t stick. When you turn the camera on, the LED screen displays a 10-second countdown before you close the door.

You have plenty of options when setting up the camera via the Strike Fore Wireless app. I recommend running the camera on Medium photo quality with High video. Avoid the Ultra-quality setting for both photo and video to save battery life, as the quality is plenty good without it. All images are delivered in HD, so there are no grainy thumbnails or waiting for the camera to trigger again to view a high-resolution photo. Videos with audio are ultra-clean. The camera took very few false triggers, and I love the user-adjustable flash.

Industry observers note that over 60 days in the field, Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV captured deer, day and night, in the center of the frame from 10 feet to 120 feet. Browning lists a detection range of 100 feet, but this camera exceeds that distance.

Using just 8 standard alkaline batteries, camera life was excellent, holding at around 90 percent after 60 days afield. At night, the MAX HD DV uses Illuma-Smart technology to adjust the flash for crisp, clear nighttime images, and its detection range remains over 100 feet after dark. This trail camera was built to handle extreme weather and keep delivering images.

Sources indicate that the only area Browning Trail Cameras needs to improve upon is its Strike Force Wireless app. The app functions well but struggles to categorize photos in the main image Library when you’re running more than one camera.

Other than that, Browning’s fresh MAX HD DV is everything I want in a cellular trail camera. It captures HD photos and 1080p video with audio, doesn’t spook deer, and has given me zero hassles after 60 days afield. It’s a tad pricey, but you’ll more than make up for it in batteries.

Moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar is the best solar-powered cellular trail camera I’ve ever used, and, at $169.99—including the solar panel—it is priced right. The panel itself is simple and effective; it slides and locks into the top of the camera, and you can angle the it to ensure it gathers as much sunlight as possible throughout the day.

I’ve had two Edge 4 Solar cameras in the field longer than any other cellular trail camera in this year’s test. They were the first cameras delivered to my doorstep, and when I get a newly introduced product, I like to start using it right away. Using Moultrie’s $50 (aftermarket) Power Mag II battery pack in tandem with the solar panel, my battery life has never dipped below 80 percent. This means you can stay out of the woods and reduce your human footprint, which is the main goal of cellular trail cameras.

Sources indicate that setup is super easy. Like all the trail cameras in this year’s test, the Edge 4 Solar connects to the strongest available cellular network. I like the newly introduced internal interface. The white push up/down, on/off button is gone. Moultrie added a twist-and-turn dial that doesn’t stick. The battery life indicator is back, and once powered on, all three lights (Not Connected-red, Connecting-yellow, Connected-green) turn solid. Then, the Connecting light flashes slowly, and after about one minute, the green Connected light turns solid green. At this point, the camera is fully operational. It pairs seamlessly with Moultrie’s app and is one of the most user-friendly cellular trail cameras in this year’s test.

Aside from the latest interface, Moultrie made other changes that earned the new Edge 4 Solar our top honor. The most notable is better nighttime image quality and a reduction in false triggers. Moultrie’s new Night Clarity feature uses enhanced low-glow IR LEDs to help illuminate the backdrop and boost edge-to-edge sharpness. Nighttime images are excellent, and every image, day or night, is delivered in HD.

Last year, especially toward the end of my 60-day testing period, my Edge 3 started triggering when nothing was there. The Edge 4 Pro Solar has not followed suit.

Sources indicate that another newly introduced and purposeful feature is Buck Shot. Moultrie AI technology detects mature bucks and sends a zoomed-in, max-resolution image. I really enjoyed this feature. Typically, action on my lease doesn’t heat up until mid-October, as few bucks summer on the property. However, this year has been different. A pair of shooter bucks—bucks I passed last fall—are semi-regular on an oat field. The Edge 4 Solar sends me a zoomed-in picture every single time either buck trips the camera.

In a partnership with onX, Edge 4 cameras are instantly pinned the second they are placed. By the end of September, I will have multiple trail cameras—cellular and conventional—spread across the West and Midwest. Too often, I get in a hurry and forget to drop a camera pin when I’m using trail cameras. However, if I’m using Moultrie, I can forget, and the map-pinning technology saves me.

Sources indicate that other standout features of the Edge 4 Solar include a tough-as-nails housing with an IP67 waterproof rating. Both of my Edge 4 Solar cameras have been exposed to torrential downpours and hail. Not a drop of moisture has gotten inside, and after months in the field, the cameras and the panels look like they just came out of the box.

Industry observers note that at under $80, SpyPoint’s Flex-M2 is a solid cellular trail camera. It comes with a two-year warranty, and SpyPoint offers a pair of M2s for just $129.99, which is an excellent deal.

Industry observers note that my first experience with the Flex-M2 was in Montana while helping a buddy set up his whitetail property. The Flex-M2 is compact, lightweight, easy to set up, and connects to the strongest cellular network in the area. Its .4-second advertised trigger speed proved accurate and reliable in my testing, and the camera captured deer at distances beyond 90 feet.

Sources indicate that when I returned from Montana, I added a pair of Flex-M2 cameras to my Colorado property. Both have been on the property for 60 days and send crisp images and 1080p video with solid audio to my phone daily. They have withstood torrid summer heat, rain and hail, and continue to impress me.

One matter I’ve had with both cameras is battery life. Using standard AA alkaline batteries, both Flex-M2 models drained relatively quickly. That said, when I swapped the battery trays for SpyPoint’s LIT-22 rechargeable power packs, battery life improved significantly. Set to Photo-only mode with medium photo resolution and a multi-shot setting of two images per trigger, my battery life has been holding steady above 80 percent.

Recent findings suggest that setup and connection time was straightforward and quick. I like the positive bottom latch lock, and the raised, gridded on/off switch is easy to operate. Once clicked on, the cellular lights blink until the camera receives a signal. Next, the status light turns blue. Once connected, the blue LED extinguishes, and the green LED on the outside of the camera blinks for 10 seconds. Once the green light stops flashing, the camera is in transmission mode.

According to recent reports, the Flex-M2 was the smallest cellular trail cam in this year’s test, and the long antenna is detachable for easy transport. Once you place your M2 in the field, it immediately reveals up on the SpyPoint app map feature.

The camera occasionally produces false triggers, but I was able to reduce this by setting the sensitivity to Medium, and the camera still picks up deer-sized game beyond 90 feet. The BuckTracker feature has done its job. Buck pics are slugged correctly, and I’ve yet to have the technology slug a doe as a buck. BuckTracker even correctly identified and a 3-inch spick at 64 feet.

In the end, Spypoint’s Flex-M2 gets our 2026 Best Value award because while it might not have all the bells and whistles of other cell scouters, it does the job—and does it for about half the price of several others.

Sources indicate that last year, Tactacam’s Reveal Ultra took home top honors in our cellular trail camera test. Its predecessor, the Reveal Pro 4.0, nearly earned the cell-cam maker a repeat performance, but fell just a tad short. It is, however, a cell scouter that every hunter should take a close look at.

Recent findings suggest that like the Ultra, the Pro 4.0 features Low-Glow and No-Glow flash settings. I love this option. Low-Glow works great for fields, logging roads, or any camera location where detection range needs a bump. No-Glow is ideal for tight timber trail crossings, river crossings, scrapes, or any area where detection range matters less and stealth matters more. The Reveal Pro 4.0 doesn’t spook deer. When set in No-Glow, deer don’t even glance at the camera, and fresh Dual Image Sensors improve day and nighttime photos.

Another stealth boost is that the slight click that previous Reveal models produced when capturing a nighttime image is gone. According to Reveal, the Dual Sensors—one stacked on top of the other—produce cleaner nighttime images without the audible click associated with a low-light filter. Once you set the Reveal Pro 4.0 in the woods, it’s a ghost, which is just what you want.

In a recent development, battery life on last year’s Ultra model was solid and given that the Reveal app lets users select camera sensitivity levels between 0 and 9, false triggers have always been few and far between. However, Reveal wanted the Pro 4.0 to have a longer run time, especially when battery-draining features such as larger image sizes, longer video durations, and Live View Mode are used.

The battery-life boosting answer is Reveal’s FlexPack R5 and R10 Power Systems. The fresh interface location on the camera’s right side, in the upper-right corner, lets the bottom of the camera (the battery box) pull away. The design was well thought out and is an overlooked feature of the new Pro 4.0. With the battery box removed, aftermarket R5 (5,000 mAh) and R10 (10,000 mAh) Power Systems plug in much like rechargeable batteries found on power tools.

Recent findings suggest that I ran the camera for 15 days using standard Alkaline AA batteries and for 15 days using the FlexPack R5. There is no question the Power Systems increase battery life and are worth the money. During its 15-day run time, the 4.0 with R5 triggered 332 times. I requested 28 videos and purposely activated Live View 10 times to further test battery life. At the end of the test, the camera still had 95 percent battery life remaining.

One small blip with this camera is that of all the cellular models I tested, the Pro 4.0 had the slowest connection time. I ran a pair of Pro 4.0s, and the average time from powering on the cameras to receiving my first test photo in an area with 4 bars of AT&T 5G LTE service was 12 minutes. I’m not sure what that was about, but both cameras struggled to get a signal and start transmitting images. Once the camera were fully connected, though, trigger speed was excellent, detection range was spot-on, and images and videos were clear and colorful.

Industry observers note that if it weren’t for the SpyPoint’s crazy-low price, Stealth Cam’s Deceptor Max 3.0 would have won our Best Photo Quality and Best Value awards. At just under $120, this cellular trail camera should be on every hunter’s radar. Past Stealth Cam cellular models I’ve test produced too many false triggers and had relatively poor battery life. Not so with this one. After 60 days in the field, the Deceptor Max 3.0 has sent only three images to my phone that didn’t show a deer, thanks to the camera’s new False Trigger Filter feature, and after 723 photos and 23 20-second videos, the battery is at 90 percent.

With its No Glow flash, the Max 3.0 has not spooked deer, near or far. Trigger speed is excellent, and with the Command app and the camera set to Standard blur reduction, images have been crisp and clean. The camera captured a doe blazing past at 1:30 a.m. in the center of the frame. The doe was in focus, and 15 seconds later, so were a pair of coyotes hot on her trail.

It has been revealed that the Deceptor Max 3.0 lets people set photo quality to 50MP. That makes for really good pics, but it’s more than most folks need and eats up battery life. I tested the camera at 4MP and 8MP, and the Max 3.0 produced the clearest, brightest, and most colorful images in this year’s test.

Recent findings suggest that A cool feature that Stealth Cam added is Rack Alert, which sends a message to your smartphone letting you know the exact moment a racked deer steps in front of your Max 3.0. This feature worked great on my Colorado lease, and my Oklahoma buddy purchased three Max 3.0 cameras and set them over feeders. He told me he never looks at his image library until Rack Alert informs him. He trusts the technology, and so do I.

Upgraded antenna pulls poor cell service.

The solar cord is big, long, and clunky.

The Interceptor is not upcoming for this year, but it one of our favorites from last year’s test, winning our Best Trigger Speed award. Covert upped its game 2025, producing a new solar cell cam scouter that’s lightning fast and offers tons of great features. The Interceptor Solar was easy to set up. Downloading the Covert app, building an account, and getting the cam operational took less than five minutes.

It has been revealed that the camera’s paddle-style antenna proved rigid and robust, even in heavy winds. Covert lists the trigger speed at .4 seconds, but my testing highlighted an average of .24 seconds. That data was obtained using two different stopwatches, as well as a chip time card that runners use.

When charged to full, the camera’s on-board solar keeps the unit running, even in dense timber. Several times, the Interceptor got down to less than 30 percent battery life at night, but it would still center images in the frame, and deliver good-qualiy photos and real-time 2K video. During the day, even without direct sun exposure, battery life would rise to 80 percent. When set on a pond and alfalfa plot, the battery never dipped below 60 percent and would achieve a full charge during the day.

In a recent development, covert lists the effective flash range at 90 feet, and my testing confirmed this. I appreciate the 2-inch screen, though very little of the actual setup work is accomplished using the camera. Everything is done in the Covert app. The Covert Interceptor Solar features on-board GPS, so you can’t lose your camera, uses 8 AA batteries as backup, and comes with a 2-year warranty.

My only complaint on this otherwise excellent camera is the long and bulky cord that connects the on-board solar unit to the camera. Be sure to take some Gorilla tape or some zip-ties to roll the cord up and tuck it out of the way. But that’s the end of my quibbling. The camera took only 11 false images during its 20-day testing period and captured a full-sprint coyote in the center of the frame, with no blur. The camera does have species recognition, which works well, but it is a service that costs extra, and I would deactivate it. Like most hunters, I know what a doe and buck deer look like.

Requires a minimum of two cameras.

Longer setup and deployment time.

Cuddeback continues to offer it’s CuddeLink system. The nice thing about Cuddelink is that once you have the Home camera and a cellular plan, you can run as many as 24 cameras on that same plan, which sarts as low as $10 per month. I opted for the $40 plan to receive unlimited photos. I tested the CuddeLink L-Series Cell Home unit ($130) and CuddeLink L-Seires cell cam ($150), so my initial investment was more. Still, I could add additional CuddeLink-compatible cell cameras (up to 24) to my $40 per month plan.

Operationally, the Home (CuddeLink) and Remote (L-Series) systems are sound. However, you’ll need to read heavy instruction manuals to get them linked to the same chain and go through the settings. It’s not a problem, and it’s not difficult. However, it will take you some time to learn the ins and outs of the system. This duo took much longer to learn about and get in the field than other cameras. That said, one the initial system is setup, it’s easy to add more cams and daisy chain them into the system.

Sources indicate that the CuddeLink L-Series comes in multiple models. I tested the Zoom IR. The photo quality is only decent, but what I do like about the camera is that it uses a center-angle Fresnel lens that increases detection range and zooms the photo in. I’m not in love with having the Home camera and then linking cameras to it, especially cellular, but the system does work and does have the potential to save you money.

Internal screen viewer to aid setup.

Among the most simple setups in the test.

Night pics suffer a bit at longer ranges.

This camera is not new by any means, but don’t let that stop you. High-quality photos, a lightning-fast trigger, and easy setup are a significant pluses with the CelluCore Live. The impressive 0.2-second trigger speed helps capture sharp images and can keep up with fast-moving deer. Plus, the fast image recovery time and subtle infrared flash elevate this cam to the next level. The only thing keeping this camera from the top models is a moderate detection range, and the data prepares are, well, not much. It’s not cheap either, though you may be able to find deals.

It has been revealed that thanks to some fantastic friends, I have access to over 700 acres of prime Colorado whitetail dirt, which has proven to be the perfect testing ground for our annual cellular trail camera test. There are plenty of deer to get pictures of and a combination of summer heat, thunderstorms, wind, and extreme temperature fluctuations tests the cameras’ durability.

Sources indicate that since I conducted last year’s cellular trail camera test, I had all the apps on my smartphone. All I did was add cameras, adjust sensitivity levels, check connectivity, and dial in the settings. For testing, I set all cameras to photo resolutions between 4 and 8MP, 1080p video, and two images per trigger.

In a recent development, before field deployment, I tested all the cams in my backyard. I wanted to make sure they paired with their corresponding app and that photos were transmitting. I set cones at measured distances and walked, jogged, and sprinted past each camera at 10-foot intervals, from 20 to 120 feet. I repeated this process in the field as well. I tested trigger speed and detection zines during daylight and nighttime hours.

In the field, I rotated all the cameras between four areas: a three-way trail intersection, the lower end of an alfalfa plot, a pond, and a community scrape deer use year-round. Throughout the test—over the course of 60 days—I evaluated each camera’s durability, ease of setup, price, battery life, image and video quality, detection range, and trigger speed. Finally, when all the testing and evaluating is done, I picked our winners.

Sources indicate that ease of setup and quick connection to the camera’s corresponding app save time and frustration. Not every hunter is a tech wizard, and thanks to the simplicity of this year’s camera crop, you don’t have to be. The only camera I had to fight with in terms of connectivity and transmission was the Reveal Pro 4.0. However, that fight was minor.

Industry observers note that many cell-cam makers are skipping grainy thumbnails and going straight to all-HD all the time. I like this. Cell cams have made me very impatient. When I get a picture of a buck, I don’t want to download a grainy image to my computer and then study it for hours trying to determine whether the buck is a shooter while I wait for a high-resolution image to come through. Cams that automatically send hi-res pics get bonus points in my book. Choose a cellular trail camera that lets you adjust image and video quality and set both high enough to avoid compromising image quality but not so high that battery life suffers.

In a recent development, trigger speed matters, especially during the rut. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have rapid trigger speed, quicker recovery times, and some type of anti-blur technology. Summertime deer don’t often test a camera’s trigger speed, but during the rut, when a doe comes running past, you want that doe centered in the frame, and the camera needs to recover fast enough that the significant buck hot on her heels gets his picture taken too. The cellular trail cameras I tested this year have fast triggers and quick recovery times.

I prefer cellular trail cameras with an adjustable flash. Some come with adjustable flash settings, while others adjust the flash setting automatically based on the time of day. Stay away from high-glow LEDs and any cell camera that produces a flash that spooks deer. All the cameras I tested this year didn’t bother deer a bit.

Cellular trail-cam manufacturers embellish a lot of things. One thing they don’t embellish—or at least didn’t embellish this year, is detection range. If anything, they underplayed it. Detection range is the maximum distance at which a camera will detect an object. Typically, the farther an object is from the camera, the larger it needs to be to be detected by the camera. Anything at over 100 feet is impressive.

In a recent development, I like a very basic and straightforward app that allows me immediate access to the camera’s settings. I like to try all the technologies and features of every cell camera I test. The better the app, the easier it is to swap between settings, organize photos, etc. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have fancy features. Take advantage of them and see if you find them beneficial. Some of them drain battery life; others don’t. Find out what works best for you and the area you hunt.

Simms Rip Line PRO Review: We Tested This Heavy-Duty Fishing Rain Gear in Downpours and High Winds

  • According to recent reports, enter Simms’ latest Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the company’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that simms has long been an industry staple for fishing apparel, most notably waders and outerwear. I’ve tested and reviewed many Simms products, including its Challenger lineup of rain gear. While that gear has always performed well, its target market is clear: dedicated recreational anglers. I’ve never bothered to test how Simms outerwear handles the trials and tribulations of everyday use by commercial deckhands or saltwater captains because, frankly, why would I? That’s not the audience it’s intended for, and I wouldn’t expect rain gear designed for landlocked fly anglers to hold up for someone used to hauling crab traps in salt spray and freezing rain all day.

According to recent reports, enter Simms’ latest Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the company’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen. The Rip Line Pro series forgoes much of the aesthetic and, shall we say, fanciness of Simms’ standard recreation-oriented rain gear in favor of pure, rugged functionality. From the moment you see the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs, it’s clear they aren’t meant for a hike down to your favorite blue-ribbon trout stream. Pick them up and feel them in hand, and that point is driven home. This is not casual rain gear, and it doesn’t sacrifice performance for looks. It’s designed for abuse of the highest order, the kind dished out by Mother Nature on the open sea.

So, how does it handle that? The look and feel right out of the box make a promise, but does the Rip Line Pro series deliver? To find out, I spent a few weeks putting this gear through the wringer in one of the best testing grounds I could think of: the Chesapeake Bay in late fall and early winter. Read on to see how the Rip Line Pro performed.

When it comes to testing gear, sometimes the timing doesn’t line up. Given the monthslong drought in the Mid-Atlantic leading up to my test, I was worried that might be the case here. As it turned out, that worry was misplaced. Exactly one day after the Rip Line Pro gear arrived, the forecast called for an epic deluge paired with extreme wind and storms. It was the perfect blend of miserable fishing conditions for testing rain gear. Lucky me.

Recent findings suggest that the forecast proved accurate, and the weather was extreme, almost to a fault. I spent the first few hours of the morning sheltering from lightning under a dockhouse on the water. The Rip Line Pro gear will protect you from a lot, but I don’t think “lightning strike” is on the list. Thankfully, the electrical portion of the storm passed, and I had the rest of the day to fish in a constant downpour and gusting wind.

After a few hours of fishing from a kayak in the rain and getting sprayed with salt water, the first thing I checked was the areas where most rain gear performs worst: the wrists, neck, and ankles. These are typically the hardest spots to protect because they offer a direct path for water to get beneath the rain gear, and they still need to allow some comfort and range of motion. The Rip Line Pro did an outstanding job of keeping moisture out of all three. The wrists and forearms were the most impressive. They feature an extended 1-millimeter neoprene cuff beneath the outer layer that lets this jacket perform almost like a full dry top. Not only does it keep rain out, but the neoprene cuff creates a seal that kept water from flowing down the sleeve even when my arm was fully submerged. I was equally impressed by the neck. While it doesn’t have the full neoprene seal of the sleeves, the hood design and zipper-and-Velcro combination created an impressively form-fitting seal that kept water from dripping down my back or chest. Finally, the ankle cuffs on the bibs did an excellent job of keeping spray and rainwater away from my feet. I was wearing ankle-height deck boots, and the leg cuffs paired perfectly with them to create an angled seal where no water could enter.

Next, I inspected the storage, namely the various dry pockets on both the jacket and bibs. Each has a well-designed, easily accessible exterior pocket sealed by a watertight zipper and tucked beneath a Velcro storm flap for extra protection. Exterior pockets on rain gear are always a gamble, but accessible waterproof storage is important. The pockets on the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs performed exceptionally well, even after I opened and closed them many times throughout the day to reach various items. Nothing seeped through the pockets to the interior of the suit, and the pockets kept everything inside them dry and functional.

Dry storage and adjustable cuffs matter, but ultimately the most important job of rain gear is keeping you dry all day long. While I was impressed with how well the Rip Line Pro kept water out of various areas throughout the day, the real test would be how wet and cold I got after fishing in rain and wind for upward of 12 hours.

Sources indicate that the answer? Not very. For me, the most impressive part of this gear is the overall protection it offered from the elements. After we returned to the boat ramp and loaded our gear, it was time to strip off the rain suit and inspect the damage. No matter how dry you think you are, a bit of unforeseen moisture usually gets through any rain gear after a long day. Apart from a few wet spots where my shirt had been exposed during the day, I was basically bone-dry. The jacket and bibs also did a great job of blocking wind chill. I had underestimated how well that was working during the day, but looking back, I realized how much the gear kept the wind from affecting my comfort. Not that I needed confirmation, but watching my fishing partners shiver miserably and wring out sopping undershirts provided a sense of warm relief, both physically and emotionally.

Recent findings suggest that protection from the elements, plain and simple. I’ve worn many bibs and rain jackets over the years, some designed for comfort and others for function. The Rip Line Pro does the best job I’ve found of marrying the two, though function is still clearly the priority.

Once you’re fully suited up, this rain gear makes you feel practically invincible, protected by an impenetrable shell of armor. I’m not saying it’s bulletproof, but I could feel an unrealistic sense of confidence building while I wore it. The materials not only kept me bone-dry through a full day of torrential rain but also provided exceptional wind protection during gusts upward of 30 knots. When it comes to protection from extreme water and wind, the Rip Line Pro series is as good as it gets.

With extreme weather protection as the focus, it’s easy to understand why some other features take a back seat. That stated, there are still a few areas I’d like to see Simms improve.

The most noticeable is the lack of mobility. The four-layer construction and fully waterproof material make this gear weatherproof, but they also make it rather cumbersome. Simms added articulation points and adjustable areas where possible, but there’s still room for improvement. At times, I felt a bit like a piece of vacuum-sealed meat, or a video game character bolted into a mech suit. Yes, I felt invincible, but I also had a harder time than I care to admit squatting to grab a sandwich from the cooler.

Sources indicate that insulation is another area that could be better. The Rip Line Pro gear does an incredible job of protecting you from water and wind, but it doesn’t have much interior insulation for true winter use. That’s easy to offset by layering proper cold-weather clothing underneath, but I could see a built-in cold-weather liner helping. Perhaps Simms will release a “winter” edition of the Rip Line Pro in the future with a wool liner or something similar.

The Rip Line Pro series of rain gear is not for everyone. In fact, I would say the target market for this gear is fairly narrow. Most casual anglers and outdoor enthusiasts can get by with less extreme, less expensive rain gear and never have an issue. While this gear is fantastic at keeping you dry, I could see it being overkill for an after-work outing during a light summer shower.

However, what the Rip Line Pro series is designed to do, it does extremely well, and the people who need this type of gear will appreciate it. The Rip Line Pro series is built for serious anglers and people who spend as much time on the water as on dry land. As with any gear in the fishing space, the more purpose-built something becomes, the less universal appeal it tends to have. That noted, if you fish as much as I do, serious rain gear becomes less a matter of convenience and more a matter of necessity. The Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs offer the type of performance and functionality I value, and I’m sure many other anglers, deckhands, and charter captains who try them will agree.

The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

It has been revealed that hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

In a recent development, on my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!).

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

It has been revealed that although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

Recent findings suggest that while there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

It has been revealed that lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

In a recent development, weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

According to recent reports, getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

It has been revealed that traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s vital to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Recent findings suggest that over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

This fall, I bought a private-land-only tag to hunt deer with my bow in South Dakota — even though I had no access to private land, nor had I ever been to the area that I planned to hunt. My plan was to knock on doors asking for permission to hunt and camp on a landowner’s property. While this sort of adventure — relying on permission for an entire hunt in unknown territory — occurs less frequently than it did years ago, I was pleased to discover that it is still possible.

Once I secured permission, the next challenge would be getting within bow range of a deer.

Industry observers note that over the course of three days in mostly wide-open country, I found myself moving through the perfect puzzle-solving experience that deer hunters are so fond of: locating deer, then figuring out how to hunt them. On the first day, I found deer. On the second day, I nearly pulled the trigger on a shooter buck. And on the third day, I sent an arrow at the biggest buck I’d ever shot.

And while the hunt unfolded perfectly, the recovery was a different story. To see how it all played out, watch the video from my hunt above.

We Tested Heated Gloves to Find Which Ones Actually Keep Your Hands Warm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • It has been revealed that the development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear.
  • Industry observers note that wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

It has been revealed that the development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear. As much as we enjoy spending time in nature during the winter months, we hate cold hands. It’s hard to concentrate on your hunt or effectively work if your fingers are so cold you can no longer feel them. For anyone with arthritis or other hand pain, it can be downright painful to venture out in winter. Luckily, battery-operated heating elements are here to change the game.

Industry observers note that wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore. That’s why we’ve done the homework for you. It doesn’t matter if you need something for work or for ice fishing, we’ve got you covered with the best heated gloves available for cold weather.

When it comes to battery life, the Ororo heated gloves—which feature three heat settings—performed better than I expected. I was able to run the gloves on the maximum temperature setting for approximately three to four hours and on the medium setting for at least five. However, the low setting was where they really shined. These gloves ran for a solid eight hours on that setting. Because they were so warm even without turning on the electricity, I highly doubt I’ll ever use the medium and high settings.

My only real complaint is that I feel the dexterity could be better. The insulation makes the fingers a bit too fat for shooting a rifle or shotgun. But the grip on the palms and fingers has a tacky feel to it that’s perfectly suited for working with shovels or other hand tools where super fine control isn’t needed. I’ll be using these to clear the driveway of snow once winter returns to Michigan. These gloves would also be excellent for operating a tractor, ATV, or snowmobile in cold temperatures.

The Savior gloves are plenty warm without an electric feature. But they also feature larger 2200 mAh batteries that help keep your fingers toasty through longer days outdoors. Because they are waterproof and thick, you can wear these gloves whenever there is snow or slush on the ground. The windproof quality makes them an excellent choice for work or riding a motorcycle, too. They are thick, so there is some dexterity loss. But Savior Heat made the button for heat control quite large, so you can easily operate it without removing the gloves.

Industry observers note that these gloves are a hair on the expensive side. But that’s to be expected for this battery size and durability. While we like these gloves best for work—like construction or ranch work—they are versatile enough to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios.

Surprisingly, there are not a lot of dedicated hunting gloves featuring electronic heating. This pair is both windproof and waterproof—perfect for hunters who don’t like to head in once the weather takes a turn for the worst. The 7.4V battery packs will help the warming functions last through a full day in frigid temperatures, and the buttons are large enough that you can operate them while wearing the gloves. Plus, they have fingertips that can operate a touchscreen.

The three heat settings allow you to customize just how warm your hands are (and the soft cotton material is extra cozy). However, we wish there were more camo patterns other than Realtree Edge. Not that the deer will notice or care, but some of us like our camo outfits to match.

In a recent development, the Snow Deer gloves offer surprising dexterity for thicker gloves. They are suitable for everything from hunting to motorcycling thanks to the sheep leather palms that help provide additional grip. The heated wires in this pair of gloves extends completely to each of the fingers, making them a great option for anyone with arthritis or circulation challenges in the hands. There is also fleece in the glove liners to help retain heat and repel moisture.

Industry observers note that these gloves have a shorter battery life than some of the other options on this list. But they’re very well constructed. Features like the sheepskin palm and fleece lining add a lot of additional value for the money here. If you need gloves that are versatile for more than one outdoor activity, these are the ones to consider.

These featherweight gloves offer a great deal of dexterity that’s ideal for work or recreational activities in bitter cold conditions. The extra reinforcement of the palm and inside of the fingers further emphasizes the fact that these gloves are made with cold weather activities in mind. You can also cinch the cuff tight to prevent extra snow and wind from getting in at the wrists and dropping your core body temperature.

These heated gloves have a slightly shorter run time than we’d expect for a battery of this size. It runs for about two hours on high, three hours on medium, and five hours on low. Extra batteries are a necessity if you need them super toasty for long periods. That said, we think the shortened runtime is a decent tradeoff for the extra dexterity offered by these gloves.

According to recent reports, for the gloves I tested, I first made sure the batteries were fully charged. I then ran each pair on the highest warmth settings to assess the battery life of each glove. I also wore the gloves while performing a variety of activities both recreational and for work. This allowed me to evaluate the comfort and dexterity of each pair. Additionally, I considered the following factors when making my decisions:.

According to recent reports, there are a few different types of heated gloves. The most popular style utilizes an electronic battery system and heated wires in the fabric, which is extremely effective for staying warm. The downside is that gloves like this are often expensive and require frequent recharging. Most have a battery life of six to eight hours depending on the set intensity level.

According to recent reports, there are also gloves and mittens with small pockets for chemical hand warmers. One pro to this style is the reduced cost. Of course, you can only use the disposable hand warmers once before tossing them in the trash. There’s also waste from the airtight wrappers this style of warmer is sealed inside, so it’s not exactly the greenest solution out there. But you don’t have to worry about charging any batteries and you can promptly replace the warmers in the field once they lose heat.

It has been revealed that when picking a glove, think about how you strategy to use it. Thicker gloves are great if all you plan to do is ride a snowmobile or ATV. However, they can promptly become useless if you need to do more delicate tasks. Thick gloves can make it difficult to squeeze the trigger on a rifle or work on an engine. Think about dexterity and how much you’ll need. At the same time, be careful not to buy gloves that are too small or too tight.

For gloves that will be used primarily for working, it pays to go with thicker materials like leather that are built to take abuse. Ideally, the palms will be reinforced for heavier tasks like ranch work. It’s not a bad idea to go for work gloves that are waterproof—or at least water-resistant—either.

Many clothing manufacturers are now making their gloves with at least one specialized fingertip designed for operating a screen. The quality of these fingertips varies depending on the glove. Some gloves just don’t have the dexterity for typing or sending emails effectively. But quality ones make for great hunting gloves when you want to stay in touch with your buddies without losing any warmth.

Mittens are almost always warmer than gloves, and that includes heated mittens. This is simply because mittens allow your fingers to share warmth and slow heat loss. Of course, this comes at the cost of dexterity for more precise tasks.

Recent findings suggest that it can be a bit of a balancing act to find the right fit for warm gloves. Go with gloves that are too loose and you lose dexterity and warmth. If the gloves are too tight, they might cut off circulation. The ideal solution is to find gloves that fall somewhere in between. The gloves shouldn’t be so tight they feel restricting, but they also shouldn’t fall off your hands.

Waterproof capabilities vary from glove to glove. Some have that feature built in standard while others may need to be kept out of the snow and ice to function properly. Be sure to read the fine print on any pair you buy first. Most work gloves are built rather ruggedly and will handle a little water.

While the technology for heated gloves continues to improve, the Ororo gloves were a standout for us in terms of battery life. These large versatile gloves will get you through the worst sub-zero temperatures that nature can dish out, and the competitive price makes them a solid option for gearing up for another long winter. Even if you choose another pair on this list, the best heated gloves will keep your digits nice and warm all season long.

#125003. Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1344 w)

Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list.
  • It has been revealed that yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak.
  • Industry observers note that for 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list. Its classic flooded hardwoods and bayous along with the state’s rich rice and grain fields, lure massive flights of puddle ducks and geese to its hallowed waters every year. This has made Arkansas stand out above other southern states as the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway.

It has been revealed that yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak. A historic drought has many duck hunters worried ahead of the Nov. 21 opener, as the serious lack of water could bring duck hunting to a standstill. Duck hunters on both public and private land may have some serious decisions to make to safeguard ducks and future duck seasons.

Industry observers note that for 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades. Every corner of the state is under a severe drought status, with some areas being more than 20 inches behind in cumulative rainfall totals.

To put the drought in perspective, this is slated to be the state’s third-driest October through January since record keeping began in 1895.

This leaves the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission with very little water to spare, to the point where the agency expects it will only be able to flood around 40 of its more than 70 moist-soil public-land hunting units.

According to recent reports, “In my 50 years of duck hunting in Arkansas, I don’t remember it ever being as dry as this,” says Brent Birch, founder of Arkansas’ Greenhead magazine. “It’s been this way all summer and well into the fall. And even with the prospects of a Super El Niño, we have nothing the forecast that says it’s going to resolve anytime soon.”.

Without an incredible amount of rainfall in a short amount of time, Birch and other waterfowlers around the state are worried not only about not having places to hunt, but that the ducks may not even show up.

Industry observers note that “So far, we are seeing a few groups of gadwalls, pintails, and other early migrating ducks but not in anything close to their usual numbers,” Birch claims. “And when it comes to incoming mallards, you can pretty much forget it. It’s just too dry for them. The fact is the closer it gets to 2027 under these conditions, the worse the entire duck season is going to be. And if we don’t start getting some wet weather soon to push ducks down here, we’re looking at a poor outlook for the entire season.”.

The reason that Arkansas waterfowl hunting is so good is that it lies at the north end of the historic feeding grounds for ducks and geese in the Mississippi Flyway. Once the cold sets in around their spring and summer breeding grounds in Canada, the birds come south to binge on Arkansas’ rich wetlands throughout the winter. However, with the current drought, the fear is that the incoming ducks will be forced to fly elsewhere.

Sources indicate that “Ducks coming south to Arkansas aren’t like ducks in northern states,” claims Ducks Unlimited Arkansas regional biologist Jake Spears, who lives in Jonesboro. “Northern birds are more apt to feed in dry fields so long as they have a body of water to roost on nearby. However, in the Southern U.S., they stop feeding in fields and primarily feed in water. They look for things like water plants and waste grains in flooded fields, which Arkansas presently just doesn’t have.”.

Spears worries that many ducks are going to fly to Arkansas and then be forced to turn northward again or keep driving south.

“The ducks need food so they may go to Louisiana, or Kansas, or Missouri — wherever they can find that food source,” says Spears. “Which is going to leave both public-land duck hunters and even most hunting clubs just completely out of luck.”.

Industry observers note that private-land duck-hunting clubs are a popular option for many Arkansas hunters and visiting nonresidents, as even during droughts, most clubs can pump water to create duck habitat and attract birds. The 2026 drought has been so bad, however, that many clubs won’t even have the water to pump.

This is especially troubling to some public-land waterfowl hunters, who worry that the private hunting clubs that can still pump water may end up attracting what few ducks do make it to Arkansas. This could result in a season that benefits the haves over the have-nots.

“I think hunting clubs are the only thing that’s going to make Arkansas appealing for ducks right now,” Spears indicates. “Most of the smaller rivers, sloughs, and backwaters we have on public land can be walked across in flip-flops right now. So the clubs that have the option to flood fields and create habitat are where the birds are going to be. But with the water table so low, clubs with the ability to pump will be few and far between, so any ducks that do show up during the season are going to have to be babied quite a bit.”.

The fact is that if the drought continues in Arkansas, duck hunters on both public and private land alike are going to have to weigh their priorities. Drought conditions are going to be tough on ducks that migrate through Arkansas, and hunting pressure will make surviving the migration harder even for birds that aren’t killed.

This leaves duck hunters with a choice to make.

Sources indicate that “It’s going to come down to responsible management on all sides because if we want to maintain the ducks we have, we have to be careful with them,” Birch says. “There are several components to management. It’s not just hunting and the noise of guns, we must be careful disturbing the ducks in any capacity. Your vehicle is an issue because you’re going to bump ducks going in and out of your hunting area, and you’re going to have to be real careful with how many days you hunt and how many hours you hunt in a day, because you’re going to have to let the birds rest.”.

With Arkansas’ duck season lasting a total of 51 days with two relatively short splits, hunters looking to limit out consistently are going to be putting serious pressure on what will already be a limited resource.

So instead of hunting hard, both Birch and Spears recommend self-imposed bag limits and time on the water so that the resource can continue to both be conserved and shared.

Sources indicate that “My suggestion to any duck hunter in Arkansas is that if you have ducks on your property, take care of them,” notes Spears. “With the limited resources, they aren’t going to be able to handle a lot of pressure. You’re going to have to limit how much you hunt and how many birds you shoot, and not be afraid to cut your hunt short. Get a few birds and then leave so the ducks can get back to the water to feed.”.

Read Next: Has Hot Cropping Ruined Duck Hunting? Here’s What the Data and Biologists Say About How Flooded Corn Affects Waterfowl Migration.

According to recent reports, while there is hope that conditions will change, the fact is that the whole of Arkansas’ 2026 duck season may be a nonstarter for many hunters. That short-term pain, however, could help future duck seasons look a little brighter. Spears and Birch are hopeful for a future where water and the waterfowl will eventually return, filling the skies and waterways like flowing veins and once again making Arkansas the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway itself.

It has been revealed that “We need to be good stewards of the resource,” urges Spears. “Hunters should do everything they can to keep [ducks] around and not shoot them off what water we do have.”.
