#125001. Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3257 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters.
  • Some big bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land.
  • But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters. A whitetail lives the 3½ years necessary to grow a bragging set of antlers by learning to cope with the annual influx of hunters during the season’s first days. Every opening day that the buck survives increases his chance of surviving the ensuing openers, as well.

Some big bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land. Others crawl into the most inaccessible and gosh-awful cover their “territory” has to offer — the kind of place hunters walk around, rather than through — and stay there until the crowds leave. And on more than one occasion, I have found a bruiser buck in a tiny, secluded patch of isolated cover — the kind of place most hunters never think to look in.

But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf. You can bet that once the steady crack of opening day rifles slackens to only an occasional pop, those big bucks will be right back to business as usual. And that is the precise reason why your best chance for bagging a wall-hanger occurs after the opening day madness has subsided.

Where you begin your search for that after-the-opener buck hinges upon one factor: the rut. Many states blueprint their firearms seasons to coincide with the rut, offering their hunters every opportunity to harvest the surplus bucks. Other states, bound in tradition, open the season after the main rut has ended. If you are planning to travel out of your home state to hunt whitetails, it makes sense to hunt a state where the season coincides with the rut, all other criteria being equal.

Sources indicate that A mature whitetail buck is a different character during the rut than he is after it. A buck’s sole purpose at that time is to procreate, and this he does with obvious enthusiasm and the stamina of a teenager. There are stories abounding in every deer camp in the country of the crazy antics performed by bucks under the spell of the “rutting moon,” such as lovesick bucks strolling across open fields in broad daylight. Others tell tales of bucks putting their noses to does’ tracks and following those tracks, even after being shot at and missed several times. Rut-crazed bucks, while under the influence of a powerful rush of hormones, have even been known to either pick fights with or attempt to mate with assorted farm livestock.

Sources indicate that so rampant are the stories that I’m afraid there exists a whole contingent of deer hunters laboring under the false assumption that all a hunter needs do to down one of these crazy buggers is to walk into the woods, lean up against a stump and wait for one of the poor, sex-addled dummies to saunter on by. Although such tactics work just often enough to keep the myth perpetuated, plenty of hunters have been sitting against stumps for more unsuccessful years than they will probably admit, and they’re still waiting for a buck to wander by.

Industry observers note that hunting whitetails during the rut and after the opening weekend of the season isn’t easy. You must employ all of the skill and woods savvy you have. Any breaks you receive because of a buck’s overactive glands should be considered a bonus.

After the opener, I refine my hunting strategy for substantial bucks by determining what stage the rut is in. This is vital because the stage of the rut will determine where I concentrate most of my midweek hunting efforts.

The whitetail buck is ready to breed long before the first doe enters estrus. During this period, the buck runs off excess energy by beating up saplings, sparring with bushes and, on occasion, duking it out with other bucks. In the process of making rubs on bushes and trees, the buck deposits scents that tell the rest of the whitetail community who was there.

Industry observers note that scrapes begin to show up in increasing numbers as the level of testosterone builds in the buck’s system. The buck paws out scrapes and leaves his scent both in the bare earth of the scrapes and on overhanging branches above the scrapes. Again, this is a means of communicating with other whitetails. The message to does is that the buck is now standing at stud, and it tells other bucks that they had best move along if they know what’s good for them.

Recent findings suggest that A buck will paw out most of his scrapes in areas where they are most likely to be seen or smelled by does. Openings in woods, old logging roads and the edges of woodlots are common places to encounter scrapes. A buck may make a dozen or more scrapes, and he’ll check some of them daily, making sure they are free of debris and liberally doused with musk/urine. These are the scrapes to hunt over.

Industry observers note that however, once the does begin cycling into heat, the dominant bucks that handle the bulk of the breeding chores are often so busy accompanying, tracking and servicing does that they neither have the time nor the need to freshen their scrapes. But if you find a string of scrapes that have not been freshened for several days, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the rut is over or that the buck that made the scrapes is hanging from someone else’s game pole. It may mean that the buck is out doing his job.

The best way to determine what stage the rut is in is to spend a day or two in the woods prior to the hunt. If fresh scrapes abound, you will be hunting the pre-coital period, and a stand near a scrape line is going to be hard to beat. If, on the other hand, you find that more than half of the scrapes are old and abandoned, it’s a good bet that the big bucks are out taking care of the does, while the lesser bucks are still hanging around their scrapes, waiting.

Sources indicate that if you just don’t have time to get into the woods prior to the season, you can get a good idea about the stage of the rut by speaking with area game managers, milk haulers, rural school bus drivers, postal carriers, loggers, trappers, farmers, grouse hunters, bowhunters or others who spend most of their time in deer country. If the bucks are chasing the does, chances are these people will have observed some of the activity.

Sources indicate that why all of the fuss over determining what stage the rut is in? Because it makes a big difference when you have to decide how you want to hunt after the opening weekend of the season.

It has been revealed that when the season begins, if the actual breeding season has not yet begun but bucks are busy pawing out new scrapes and freshening old ones, chances are the bucks will curtail this activity during the high-pressure days at the beginning of the season, resuming their rounds once the hunters thin out. I like to have at least a half-dozen scrape lines pinpointed prior to the opener, and I check them after the opening weekend for any sign of activity. I then concentrate my hunting efforts near the “hottest” scrapes.

If your pre-season scouting and snooping indicates that the actual breeding season is in progress, then hunting over scrapes may not be your best option for tagging a really good buck. Remember, it is often the big, dominant bucks in the area that handle the bulk of the breeding chores. Even in an area with an excellent buck-to-doe ratio, a breeding buck can be kept so busy that he has little time or need to tend his scrapes. Often, a buck will spend 24 hours with the same doe, breeding her several times before her cycle ends. At this time, it is the doe, not the buck, that determines where the pair will travel. Though I would not totally rule out hunting in the vicinity of inactive scrapes at this stage of the rut, there are other options that I’ve found give me a better chance at tagging a big buck.

One of my favorite methods during this period is to concentrate my hunting efforts in areas where I have encountered good numbers of does in the past. Does and fawns tend to hang around together, and they routinely congregate in specific areas, often bedding as a loosely knit group in a favorite swale or sunny hillside. I can’t direct you to these “ladies-only bedrooms,” but I’ll bet there is such a place in the chunk of woods you hunt.

Industry observers note that you can locate these places that hold special favor with the does by simply noting those areas where you encounter the most doe activity. After a few years of hunting the same ground, a familiar pattern becomes apparent.

In a recent development, on several occasions, I have located a hotbed of doe activity by simply listening to other hunters. When you hear a hunter complain that he sat on his stand and saw 15 does but not a single buck, find out where he was sitting. You can bet that when the time is right, there will be a buck or two sniffing around the vicinity.

According to recent reports, A dominant buck ranges well out of his home area during the actual breeding season. I don’t think he goes out of his way looking for does so much as he is drawn out of the territory when following the tracks of a doe that has visited his scrapes or just wandered through the area. A buck engaged in this activity moves with a single-minded purpose, shuffling along, nose to the ground, seldom looking up, intent upon finding the maker of the tracks he is following. I once missed a buck that trailed a doe past my tree stand in this manner, my arrow slicing harmlessly over the buck’s back only to skitter noisily through the carpet of dry oak leaves a few yards beyond. The buck lifted his head and looked in the direction of the commotion. Apparently satisfied that whatever had made the racket was not what he was looking for, he then ambled on his way while I frantically fumbled around trying to nock another arrow.

In a recent development, when a buck finally tracks down a doe, as often as not, she will then lead the buck on a little chase that, in all likelihood, will take the buck still farther from his home base. By the time the buck actually mates with the doe, he may be miles from his original starting point. On the way back to his core area, it is not unlikely that the buck will cut the track of another “hot” doe and repeat the scenario.

Industry observers note that all of this rambling makes it impossible to pattern a buck during the height of the breeding season, prompting many knowledgeable whitetail hunters to claim that taking a good buck during the peak of the rut is mostly a matter of luck. I disagree.

Hunting near a known “doe hangout” can help. And you can stack the deck in your favor even more by hunting a funnel area near a concentration of does. A funnel is simply any natural or man-made feature of the terrain that restricts the movement of deer. An hourglass-shaped section of woods is the classic funnel. Deer moving from one wide portion of the hourglass to the other must pass through the narrow waist. In farm country, the funnel may be a brushy fenceline connecting two woodlots. In the rugged country of the West, where whitetails are becoming increasingly common, a jutting jaw of sheer rimrock can force whitetails into a confined passage. Funnels work well because even though a buck with a snootful of “hot” doe scent wouldn’t care if he was standing in the middle of Madison Avenue, the does do not lose their heads. Does will stick to cover when on the move, even when there is a grunting, panting Romeo dogging their every move.

According to recent reports, in many whitetail states, hunters are left with no choice but to hunt well after the main rutting period is over. At first, hunting after the opening weekend under these circumstances appears to be a futile endeavor. Without the promise of the rut to keep the bucks on the move, and with the absence of hunters to jar deer loose, what chance does the midweek hunter have of scoring on a decent buck? He has a pretty good one, I would say.

First, although the bulk of the breeding chores are completed in about a two-week period, there is still some activity after the main rut is over. Does that were not impregnated will cycle back into heat 28 days after their first estrus cycle ends. In some states, this is just about the time the rifle season rolls around. In addition, in some of the best whitetail areas, it is not uncommon for female fawns of the year to breed. This often applies to as many as 40 percent of them. Frequently, these young breeders experience their first estrus cycle later than older does. So, don’t strike out the possibility of the rut working in your favor even though the peak has passed. In that part of Minnesota where I live, the bulk of the breeding is completed by mid-November, yet each year, I find active scrapes late into November and even December. Last season, during an especially mild December, I found a pair of bushel-basket-size recently freshened scrapes while hunting grouse on New Year’s Eve day. If you can find these “late scrapes,” concentrate your hunting efforts near them.

Recent findings suggest that but even if you fail to find any of these scrapes later in the year, you still stand a good chance of tagging a buck during the middle of the week if you let the after-effects of the rut work in your favor. During the rut, a buck takes little time out to eat. By the end of the breeding season, a buck that began the rut in peak condition can be drawn and thin, actually haggard looking. Some bucks lose up to 20 percent of their body weight during the course of the rut. Across the Northern states and Canada, where winter-kill is an annual problem, the big, breeding bucks follow the fawns in death each winter simply because they run off all of their reserve fat during the rut and are often unable to replenish it before the onset of winter snows.

According to recent reports, although the largest bucks are often nocturnal in their feeding habits at other times of the year, when the rut is over, dominant bucks cannot afford to limit their foraging to the hours of darkness alone. In order to regain their strength and put on the layer of fat necessary to see them through the winter, they must forage during the day. This gives the after-the-opener hunter the chance he needs to find bucks up and about during shooting hours.

Industry observers note that this need to feed heavily does not necessarily mean that a substantial buck will be found sauntering around an alfalfa field at high noon, scarfing down the last frost-tinged greens of the year. It does mean that rather than tucking himself safely away in a thicket long before the morning sun ever peeks over the ridge, a buck will now tend to linger at the feeding grounds longer in the morning. Does and fawns often feed for an hour after sunrise, and now, bucks will begin to do the same. In the evening, when they normally would not begin feeding until complete darkness had fallen, bucks will now arrive at the feeding sites earlier — often in that last precious minute of shooting light.

Industry observers note that even at midday, the major boys will not be content to simply lay in their beds and chew their cuds. I have noticed that once the rut is over, bucks are much more likely to rise from their beds and spend an hour or two at midday — often between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. — browsing near their bedding sites.

All of this daylight activity is a major plus for the after-the-opener hunter who must depend upon natural deer movements, rather than other hunters, to put a buck in front of him. The natural inclination is to hunt from a stand near the feeding area, but this is a mistake when you’re after mature bucks. A big buck is constantly alert, using each of his senses to detect the slightest hint of danger. Never is a buck more alert than when he is feeding during shooting light because he knows he is most vulnerable then. The bucks I have observed feeding during the season have been wound-up tighter than a watch spring and ready to snap at the slightest provocation. One miscue on your part, whether it is movement or scent or whatever, will send him running. I try to avoid known feeding areas, and I concentrate my efforts near the bedding areas.

Sources indicate that hunting near the bedding area means that any shot I take will most often be attempted in good light. That’s crucial for a clean kill. A buck may not arrive back at his bedding area until the sun is an hour high in the morning, and he may leave his bed to begin a dawdling trip to the feeding area in late afternoon. Instead of risking a poor shot at a shadowy form in the gray gloom of dusk or dawn, I take my shot when the light is in my favor.

According to recent reports, also, by concentrating my efforts in the vicinity of the buck’s daytime haunts, I have a better chance of catching him up and about during the midday hours. If I am forced to move into the bedding area and take a stand at mid-morning, I risk detection by the buck. But if I move into my stand in the dark and set up quietly, I double my chances of scoring. If I fail to take the buck as he returns from breakfast, I will be there waiting when he gets up for lunch or dinner.

But you don’t have to confine yourself to a stand. If conditions allow for quiet stillhunting, I like nothing better than to either prowl the edges of a buck’s daytime haunts or simply tread my way along a ridge littered with the acorns of the white oak, moving only a few yards at a time and stopping often to look, listen and feel. Often after the crowds of opening day are gone from the woods for another year, it is just me and the deer — one-on-one. And that’s the way I like it best.

Here’s Proof That You Don’t Need to Break the Bank for a Hardside Deer Hunting Blind

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Growing up, I never really hunted out of a blind.
  • It has been revealed that once I figured out the planting cycle, I knew it was time to get my hands on a hardsided blind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Growing up, I never really hunted out of a blind. Here in the Northeast, we traditionally hunt from treestands or just pick a good spot on the ground with natural cover. Sure, I watched plenty of hunting shows where they sat in a hardsided blind over a food plot, but that just wasn’t an option for me. That is, until recently, when I started planting my own food plots here in Pennsylvania.

It has been revealed that once I figured out the planting cycle, I knew it was time to get my hands on a hardsided blind. But the absurd prices of some of the higher-end models really turned my stomach. Then, I heard about the Maverick XL-V and knew it’d be a great fit for my new food plot.

Sources indicate that this six-panel blind provides a near 360 degree view with large, vertical windows that are perfect for archery hunting. It’s also quite spacious, easily allowing two people to sit and hunt comfortably. But the best part is, it’s a fraction of the price that you’d pay for some of the competition out there. Here’s what you need to know about this versatile hunting blind.

Recent findings suggest that after tending to my food plot for the better part of the summer, the clover was flourishing and my Maverick XL-V had arrived just in time to build it a month or so ahead of the season. This allowed the deer to get used to the blind’s presence prior to the season getting underway in October.

The first true test of the blind was setting it up. Maverick talked up its six-panel lock-in system, and I was excited to see how it all came together. Unfortunately, the first shipment I received was missing the door panel. After a quick call to customer support, the missing door panel arrived about a week later, but that panel was missing the window. Rather than wait any longer, I opted to simply replace the window with a piece of plexiglass cut to fit.

The good news is that the lock-in system works flawlessly. The panels all fit together promptly and seamlessly, making it easy to get the blind placed on our homemade platform with just two people. (For some of the bigger, spendier hard-sided blinds, you need a tractor or forklift.) Once it was set up, all that was left was to wait for our archery season to open.

On the opening weekend of archery, my girlfriend and I had an amazing first evening sitting in the XL-V blind. With several does and a few small bucks under 20 yards away, they never had any idea we were there. It was spacious enough for two blind chairs, our hunting packs, and our bows to fit with plenty of room to spare.

Recent findings suggest that since then, I’ve spent several weeks in and out of the blind, with deer in the plot almost every time. I have yet to see a target buck arrive in daylight, but I have a feeling the skunk will be knocked out of the blind in no time.

After spending several weeks in the XL-V, I can say I’ve grown quite fond of this blind. The windows offer a great view and operate on friction hinges, with three easy-to-use latches to keep them shut. Thus far, the windows open and close silently, which is obviously incredibly crucial to avoid spooking any deer in range.

The door offers two easy-to-use handles, too, and is large enough to fit through without having to contort my body to squeeze into the blind. Aside from the missing components with delivery, the set up was easy and straightforward. The panels with the lock-in system were intuitive and functioned as expected. I honestly expected to struggle getting it set up on our homemade platform, but was pleasantly surprised to be proven wrong.

It has been revealed that obviously, the issues I experienced with the missing door and then the missing window were not ideal. It’s hard to say if that’s a one-off and I simply got unlucky, or if there’s a larger matter at play there. Aside from that, there are a few other areas I think the XL-V could improve.

Recent findings suggest that first, the near-360 degree view is great, but it leaves you backlit on sunny days. I’d love to see included covers for the windows behind you to avoid the backlighting issue. On top of that, this blind is not airtight, meaning you need to be aware of where your scent will be going just like hunting from a treestand.

Recent findings suggest that while the XL-V might have some room for improvements, it’s worth keeping in mind how affordable this hardsided blind is compared to others on the market. It might lack some of the high-end features those blinds offer, but it still gets the job done for a fraction of the price.

In a recent development, once getting it set up and deployed in the plot, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed every sit. It’s provided me with some incredible hunts, plenty of room to stretch my legs throughout some long sits, and ensure I have all of the gear I need. If you’re in the market for a budget hunting blind, don’t overlook the Maverick XL-V hunting blind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that the best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

It has been revealed that over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to Fresh Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive.

Industry observers note that if the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

In a recent development, and the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

Recent findings suggest that the only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting.

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to latest levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

Industry observers note that the upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” noted a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”.

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some.

It has been revealed that the Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”.

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.).

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better.

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag.

Sources indicate that brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has released in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Recent findings suggest that despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

In a recent development, 40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

Industry observers note that if you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

Recent findings suggest that when assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how promptly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research highlights that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Industry observers note that running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Recent findings suggest that don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Recent findings suggest that each season, we evaluate newly introduced releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to Newly introduced Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Sources indicate that freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and indicates her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

Sources indicate that A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

Sources indicate that jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and presently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Recent findings suggest that once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Latest Update: The Hunt for the Jameson Buck, a 250-Inch Kansas Legend That Lived in an Old Strip Mine

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Ghost Buck,” appeared in the November 1991 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • The big whitetail moved steadily, head lowered, nosing a course through a lunarlike landscape of earth mounds, dark puddles and hair-thick brush.
  • Industry observers note that then abruptly the buck froze, as if gripped by an old instinct for caution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Ghost Buck,” appeared in the November 1991 issue of Outdoor Life. The Bruce Jameson buck ultimately scored 248 1/8 inches after deductions, according to Boone and Crockett. Although it was one of the top-scoring archery bucks of all time when it was killed, it’s listed as the 16th largest nontypical ever taken in Kansas. Though the story mentions Pope and Young, Jameson’s name isn’t listed among its records. The rack is now owned by Bass Pro Shops.

The big whitetail moved steadily, head lowered, nosing a course through a lunarlike landscape of earth mounds, dark puddles and hair-thick brush. Strip mining had turned the area raw and made hunting supremely difficult. Yet this giant of a buck moved on. Something compelled him, an urge perhaps. It was mid-November, the peak of the rut.

Industry observers note that then abruptly the buck froze, as if gripped by an old instinct for caution. From atop a rise, he surveyed the area.

Industry observers note that to bowhunter Bruce Jameson, who knelt against the base of a cottonwood 50 yards away, it was now clear that all of the speculation about the buck had been true. Somehow the hundreds of hunters before him who had failed to get a close look at this ghost buck had emerged with an accurate picture — perhaps because it was nearly impossible to exaggerate in describing the animal. Everything about the buck was massive. His long, heavy body seemed to melt into a neck that was a barrel of solid muscle from supporting his towering, forearm-thick antlers. The bowhunter clutched his compound Pearson Spoiler and saw his knuckles turn a splotchy white.

This buck, so well-known but seldom seen, had drawn Jameson into the woods 20 of the past 21 mornings. He had been taunted by a combination of too much distance and brush. Day after day, there had been no clear shot. Still, the bowhunter felt a kind of jubila­tion as he watched the world-class whitetail lower his head and fade into the brush. After all, he had just accomplished something no other hunter had — he had seen the ghost buck while hunting.

At the time, the walls of Jameson’s Pittsburg, Kan­sas, bowhunting and taxidermy shop were lined with major-game mounts. Most were whitetail bucks of envi­able size. Still, to a mount, they were overshadowed by one buck in particular, which, once noticed, instantly took your eyes away from the rest. Hunters had come from all parts of southeastern Kansas to marvel at this huge non-typical buck. His main beams were nearly as thick as a softball where they rose from the mount, and they thickened as they climbed into a crown of spike­ like points. When displayed at a trophy deer show, people had crowded around, labeling it the most im­pressive non-typical to come from a state that’s been dominating the record books for a quarter-century.

Equally provocative was the fact that the deer was still in the wild. The display cape was that of another buck. The gargantuan antlers had been found after the ghost buck had shed them the previous winter. It wasn’t the first time, either.

Deer hunters around town got their first hint of an exceptional horned buck when John Jameson, Bruce’s father, happened upon a shed antler during a 1987 bowhunt. Though bleached from the sun and pocked by rodents, there was no mistaking that it came from a trophy buck. The single antler was unusually massive and sported eight points.

Local hunters were surprised that no one had ever seen the buck that carried it. Many speculated that the beast had already died a natural death. The following spring though, Jameson’s nephew, Doug Kratz, discovered that the ghost was still in their presence when he happened across a massive, freshly shed antler. A few weeks later the other side, an eye­ opening set, also turned up. Together the two antlers carried a total of 22 points.

Sources indicate that the presence of the big buck in the Pittsburg area was particularly exciting to the Jamesons. Bruce Jameson is one of 10 children who grew up hunting and fishing with their father. In fact, all of the Jamesons, including their father, still bow hunt together regularly. Yet, the Jameson’s home range, southeastern Kansas, is the only area of the state not known for producing exceptional whitetail racks. Hunting pressure is high and the habitat fair at best for producing big bucks.

It has been revealed that like scores of other hunters, Jameson planned on hunting the ghost buck hard during the 1988 season, but his latest taxidermy and bowhunting shop was gaining popularity with local hunters. He couldn’t get away.

It has been revealed that jameson was determined, however, to keep his ears open while he manned his Main Street shop. The progressing season started out as a repeat of the past: no sightings, and no signs of a huge whitetail — no significant tracks, massive rubs or huge scrapes. Still, the attraction of this buck, and his mystique, seemed to build with each passing week.

There probably isn’t a deer camp or small hunting town in America that doesn’t have a legendary buck — an animal so massive, so elu­sive, so remarked upon, that his image is forever associated with something beyond the ordinary. The ghost buck is an idea more than a form, and as such, it has a special invincibil­ity. Yet Bruce Jameson was determined to change that.

According to recent reports, luck helped. Soon, Jameson’s good friend Dennis Scales accomplished something that instantly made him a local celebrity — he glimpsed the ghost buck. It was still early in the morning when Stales spotted a doe and a small buck feeding across a field of milo stubble.

From his truck, Scales could easily watch as the unimpressive pair fed across the expanse of knee-high cover. Then it happened. Scales, an avid deer hunter, watched in wonder as the significant non-typical rose from the scant cover and hurried toward the little buck and doe. As soon as the monster buck reached the doe he in­stantly flattened out, totally out of sight in what looked like open cover. It was a ritual that Scales witnessed three times before the passing of a distant pickup truck spooked the big whitetail into the woods. No one else saw the famous buck during the gun or bow season.

Industry observers note that those who’ve driven the southeastern Kansas area can understand the amazement sur­rounding the notion of a giant buck in flatlands country. With a decided absence of wilder­ ness, every mile of land is evenly gridded by gravel roads that are often traveled by small­ game hunters and fishermen, farmers and com­muters.

Despite Scales’ sighting, and the discovery of another huge shed antler, Jameson was not encouraged. “My heart would start pounding when I would look up and think of myself in a tree with him coming down the trail,” he mused. “But I knew it was going to be tough to pick one buck, a buck that you know is at least 5 1/2 years old, in an area with heavy pressure and heavy cover. I also knew that I’d hunted this area all of my life and never seen the buck. I couldn’t help but occasionally wonder if he was still alive.”.

One summer evening, Jameson found out. “I do quite a bit of looking in August,” he said. “The bucks will be hanging together, and because they haven’t been pressured you can sometimes catch them coming out to feed in the evenings.”.

Along with a cousin, Bruce drove to a soybean field in his hunting area. Most sum­mertime bucks are calm and tolerant of distant vehicles, but one buck in particular melted into the nearby woods when Jameson was still 150 yards away. That was close enough.

“I didn’t need binoculars to know it was him,” Jameson recalled. “I was in a state of awe. I just turned to my cousin and said, ‘You have no idea what you just saw — he’s one of the best in the state, probably one of the best in the nation.’ It was good to know that I’d at least get a chance to hunt him.”.

Jameson also knew that he wouldn’t be alone in his quest. The lad who’d found the most recent sheds had disclosed the buck’s location. Going into the season about a dozen bowhunters had sworn to hold out for this buck, which seemed now more flesh than ghost. In the weeks before the opening of deer season, a continuous cloud of dust hung over the dirt roads as hunters and non-hunters alike cruised along, hoping for a glimpse of the legendary buck. Then on October 1, bowhunters swarmed into the woods, but again it was as if the buck had turned to mist.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Jameson bided his time, hop­ing the upcoming rut would draw the buck out. Though Jameson had a good idea where the deer lived, he couldn’t get permission to enter the property. Instead, he set up 1 1/2 miles away and waited.

“I figured that once the rut started he’d start covering more ground,” Jameson rea­soned. “Even then I knew he’d be tough be­ cause of the terrain.”.

Deer hunting in this part of Kansas can be, well, the pits. This is coal country. In previous decades huge chunks of ground were clawed open to get at coal deposits. The strip-mined areas look like moon surface.

It has been revealed that piles of dirt from eight to 30 feet high lay interspaced with water-filled pits. Where there is dirt there is dense brush. The jungle — and swamplike strip pits offer some of the most difficult hunting in the nation.

Jameson spent his first week in a tree at the edge of “the pits” near a slough that would offer the buck the easiest and most direct route through the area. He saw only a small buck and some fawns.

According to recent reports, frustrated, he moved to an area that held a small green wheat field and a scattering of hedge trees. Though he sighted and passed up a number of lesser bucks, there was no sign of the ghost buck. The unseasonably warm and dry weather that ushered in the November rut­ — hunters in the area saw more mosquitoes than snowflakes — further tilted the odds against Jameson.

Finally, Jameson got a much needed break in the form of a light shower, which would allow him to pick up tracks. He started slowly traveling the back roads.

Industry observers note that “We often look for what we call ‘shortcut’ trails in the dust on the shoulders of roads,” Jameson explained. “They’re basically trails that substantial bucks use to cover a lot of ground and to get from section to section without being seen.”.

Recent findings suggest that the veteran hunter observed that these shortcut trails seem to be utilized only by substantial bucks, seldom by does or lesser bucks. “You’ll usually only find the tracks of one or two bucks,” Jameson added. “We check the road edges because the trails are tough to see or follow in the woods, they get used so little.”.

A few years earlier, in just such a place, one of his brothers had arrowed a trophy with a Boone and Crockett Club non-typical score in excess of 200 points.

In a recent development, jameson soon found tracks coming and going from the section he’d hunted earlier in the season. There were two sets of buck tracks: one significant, the other less so. Experience told the hunter that the larger set probably belonged to a dark-racked buck he’d seen and passed up near the wheat field.

But what about the other tracks? They weren’t overly impressive, and he couldn’t remember seeing them before. But it was their location, not their size, that excited Jameson. It was a prime spot for an old, wary buck to travel. “Maybe,” he thought, “just maybe …”.

Fired by a hunch, Jameson took a rare morning off from his treestand vigil and planned to move from his wheat field location to the slough at the edge of the pits where he’d first started.

Sources indicate that jameson had just started the walk into the slough when something caught his eye. “I looked across the field and there he was,” noted Jameson. “I could tell it was him no problem. He had his nose down bird-dogging it back and forth. He was looking for a doe.”.

Jameson’s hunch was confirmed; the buck had gone right through the slough where he’d wanted his stand. But rather than bemoan his bad timing, Jameson decided to make the best of the situation as he watched the non-typical disappear into the timber.

“A lot of hunters make the mistake of seeing a significant buck and then not doing anything about it,” noted Jameson. “We’ve taken sev­eral trophy-class bucks by swinging around and getting ahead of them. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, but I figured it was worth a try.”.

It has been revealed that the buck had been heading north, possibly toward the shortcut trail Jameson had found a few days earlier. The bowhunter wasted no time circling ahead of the buck. He ran down the trail that bisected the two sections, jumped a fence, and sprinted to the top of one of the many dirt mounds.

It has been revealed that it was a guess — hoping the buck would cross 30 yards to his right — but it was Jameson’s only chance. Even if the buck came his way he knew that the thick underbrush would make a shot next to impossible.

It has been revealed that jameson had been in place only five min­utes when he caught movement. It was the ghost buck, passing at a steady clip. The range was too long and the brush too thick. Jameson’s heart was drumming against his rib cage. He tried to sneak a few steps closer. but he couldn’t get within 50 yards.

In a recent development, then, for reasons unclear to the hunter. the whitetail suddenly stopped and raised his head. In the next moment, he was gone. disappearing over the edge of a mound. Jameson found himself staring at the scene as it was just minutes ago — that is, without the ghost buck­ — and he felt a kind of pleasurable sadness. “It was a strange feeling.” he remembered. “I’d actually figured out where he’d go, but I was also disappointed. You simply don’t get many chances at a deer like him. He sure had proven that over the past several seasons. I had to wonder whether I’d ever get another chance.”.

Feeling almost electrified, Jameson waited a few minutes before sneaking back carefully to the spot where he”d last seen the whitetail. At least, he reasoned, he could get a look at the tracks and perhaps figure out once again where the buck was heading.

Sources indicate that when he saw them, he instantly recognized the tracks — they were the smaller set he’d seen on the shortcut trail. Jameson walked in the direction the buck had taken and paused at the top of the next mound, wondering why he hadn’t seen the deer cresting one of the sea of little ridges.

Without warning, there was a loud crash. Jameson twisted around and saw the buck of his dreams jump from a hiding place 35 yards away, staying to a course that kept distance between him and the bowhunter. Instinct took over. It seemed Jameson’s hundreds of hours of indoor and outdoor shooting had somehow led him to this shot — he was ready. “I drew, got ahead of the buck, and when the time was right, I released the arrow without actually thinking about it.”.

In a recent development, jameson watched his Anderson 365 mag­num broadhead enter the buck as the animal stepped through a tiny clearing. Ironically. it was one of the rare occasions when this sharp­ shooting bowhunter had been unsure of his arrow placement. He watched the buck pause briefly atop the next mound, then move out of sight as if not seriously wounded.

At the thought of a bad hit on such a magnificent animal, Jameson fell to his knees and was sick. Long a man of deep conviction, he did what came naturally in a time of crisis — he noted a quick prayer for the animal’s fast and humane death. “I call upon God anytime I feel I need help.” he said. Then he thought to go get his father, who was waiting nearby.

Industry observers note that an hour later Jameson, his father, John, and his brother Richard were back in the area. The trio quietly surveyed the scene of the shot. There was blood. They soon found the arrow. but it was floating in a nearby pit of water, wave-cleansed of any tissue or hair.

It has been revealed that after deciding the trail looked good, the trio inched in the direction the ghost buck had taken. They saw that the buck had stopped and changed directions. The father and sons found the huge whitetail at the top of the next dump­ — barely 70 yards away from where it had been hit. Clearly, the ghost buck had succumbed within a matter of a few seconds.

Sources indicate that “When he saw the deer,” Jameson re­called of his father, “tears came to his eyes and he hugged me around the neck. He’s always had a great sense of pride in each of his six sons and our accomplishments. I’ll never forget it.”.

In a recent development, what will forever be known as the “Jameson buck” will go down as one of the most impres­sive whitetail bucks of all time. The mass of the rack was almost indescribable and, along with the skull plate, weighed an eye-opening 12 pounds.

After the 60-day drying period, the mam­moth rack scored 253 6/8 Pope and Young Club points — the tally may well go higher when scored by the club’s official panel. As it stands, the “Jameson buck” is the third largest non­ typical whitetail arrowed in history.

Recent findings suggest that A close look at the ghost buck revealed how he had lived virtually undetected by sportsmen for years. Though he field-dressed at 243 pounds, his feet sported surprisingly small hoofs. Jameson also theorized that the jungle of points on the buck’s rack may have kept him from rubbing on substantial trees. “When you really start looking at the rack you realize that he couldn’t rub all of his velvet on a big tree,” stated the hunter. “He probably had to rely on small trees or maybe even brush. It’s possible we saw his rubs and just dismissed them as those of a small buck.”.

Latest Update: ‘I Tried Not Looking at the Rack.’ Indiana Hunter Tags 199-Inch Buck on State Park Land

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that avery Fisher of Delphi, Indiana, and his best friend since high school, Nathan Van Dokkenburg, put in for an Indiana parks draw hunt on the recommendation of a buddy.
  • Sources indicate that indiana has special limited-draw, short-term deer hunts on about 25 public parks around the state.
  • Neither Fisher nor Van Dokkenburg had ever walked the park they drew to hunt, which they declined to name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that avery Fisher of Delphi, Indiana, and his best friend since high school, Nathan Van Dokkenburg, put in for an Indiana parks draw hunt on the recommendation of a buddy. Both drew the two-day Nov. 16-17 firearms season.

Sources indicate that indiana has special limited-draw, short-term deer hunts on about 25 public parks around the state. The hunts help manage the burgeoning deer herds, and most allow sportsmen to take three deer per hunt, with a limit of one buck. The number of hunters drawn for each park varies, but about 150 hunters are typically allowed on a park for each two-day hunt.

Neither Fisher nor Van Dokkenburg had ever walked the park they drew to hunt, which they declined to name. But they spent a lot of time figuring out where they should be on the property well before the hunt.

In a recent development, “We studied a lot of Google Maps and onX to get an idea where we should hunt far back in the park well away from other hunters,” Fisher tells Outdoor Life. “It’s rolling hills with significant creek drains and draws … I’ve hunted that kind of land previously, and I had a good idea where to go early that Nov. 16 opening morning.”.

The hunters checked in when the park opened at 5 a.m. and were prepared for an all day sit with packs, gear, and food.

“We got far back into the park, about one and a half miles from the road,” states Fisher, 25, who works as a financial advisor. “We stayed on ridgetops, and about one mile in, Nathan and I split up.

Fisher went about another half mile, hiking by the light of his headlamp.

Sources indicate that “In the dark I spotted a tree line that had a lot of buck rubs. Then I saw a doe, and I figured it was a pretty good place.”.

He climbed about 30 feet off the ground and settled into his saddle with his coffee and snacks his favorite .44-cal Ruger, a gift from his father years ago.

It was cold early that morning, and he heard something in a nearby ravine around 7:45 a.m.

“I thought I saw a buck and put my binoculars on it, and it was one with a good spread and nice tines about 100 yards away.”.

He raised his rifle and rested it against the tree for support while looking for the buck in his scope.

In a recent development, “But my breath kept fogging the scope,” he indicates. “I kept cleaning it with my gloves, and the deer kept getting closer … I tried not looking at his rack as he turned uphill and then I saw his sticker points as he was rubbing trees.”.

Fisher found the shoulder in his scope and squeezed the trigger. The buck ran uphill past Fisher, wobbling as it went. When the buck stopped at 60 yards, Fisher shot again. The buck dropped.

Fisher texted Van Dokkenburg and told him he’d shot a nice buck, but to keep hunting because they were allowed to shoot up to three deer apiece.

Recent findings suggest that “A group of does came in at about 9 a.m., and I shot one and it fell,” Fisher claims. “I decided not to shoot any more deer that morning.

It has been revealed that “We had to bone and pack out two deer like we were on a Western hunt. I figured that was enough for us to lug out of there that day.”.

Van Dokkenburg saw nothing to shoot and met up with Fisher about 11 a.m., filming Fisher as he first walked up to his buck and realized how huge it was.

In a recent development, “I was speechless at the size of his rack,” says Fisher. “I knew he was big, but not a rack like that. I’m grateful and thankful to the Lord.”.

Using a wheeled cart and backpacks, the two hunters hauled both deer back down to their vehicle.

“I think my pack with deer and gear weighed over 100 pounds, and I had to stop and offload more from my pack to the wheeled cart,” Fisher states.

They then drove to check in their deer with park personnel.

According to recent reports, fisher’s 13-point buck has been measured with an unofficial green score of 199 5/8 inches. It turned out Fisher’s second shot had been unnecessary, since his first had struck the heart.

The two buddies returned to the park to hunt the next day, though Fisher notes they were exhausted from the previous day’s hunt.

“We saw some deer, including another far-off buck, but we didn’t shoot another deer that second day,” he indicates. “Nathan is drawn for another two-day park hunt later this year, so he still has a good chance of taking deer, maybe even a huge buck.”.

#124991. 15 Scent Control Strategies for Deer Hunting That Actually Work

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1187 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

15 Scent Control Strategies for Deer Hunting That Actually Work

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A heavy-antlered 12-point buck materializes on the trail.
  • According to recent reports, we all know that any successful deer hunt starts with not getting busted by a whitetail’s incredibly powerful sense of smell.
  • It has been revealed that with careful scent control, you can give yourself a slight edge that just might mean the difference between getting busted and getting a shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A heavy-antlered 12-point buck materializes on the trail. He’s only five steps from bow range, but then he throws his nose in the air, goes rigid with nervousness, and waves the white flag. Game over. That’s all, folks.

According to recent reports, we all know that any successful deer hunt starts with not getting busted by a whitetail’s incredibly powerful sense of smell. And today there’s a whole collection of gear that’s marketed as being able to beat a deer’s nose. Many of the scent control gear and strategies are gimmicks, but some are not.

It has been revealed that with careful scent control, you can give yourself a slight edge that just might mean the difference between getting busted and getting a shot. Here are scent-reduction efforts that work, with 15 steps that hunters can use to minimize scent before, during, and after the hunt.

In a recent development, hunters must understand they will never completely neutralize the scent they emit. Furthermore, they will never completely beat a whitetail’s nose. However, a hunter can minimize their scent.

In a recent development, this won’t keep a deer from smelling you, but it might buy you a little extra time or a few more yards. It can also make all the difference in a non-target deer just moving along rather than alarm snorting.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to use all of the following strategies just to shoot a deer. But, implementing at least some of them will certainly make you more effective in the stand.

Industry observers note that deer hunters should consider a long-term scent control mentality. Rather than just preparing the day of the hunt, start mitigating scent long before. During hunting season, consider cutting the smelly shampoos, soaps, colognes, deodorants, and aftershaves out of your routine. This will help keep your clothes smelling more natural, too.

Sources indicate that washing your hunting clothes is the next step. Treat with scent-reduction laundry detergent. Such laundry detergent doesn’t remove all scent, but it knocks out a lot of it and it doesn’t add unnatural scents. (Also, on a deer vision note, ensure that the detergent does not contain UV brighteners.).

It has been revealed that once your hunting clothes are clean, store them in a dedicated container. A portable plastic tote that has a place at home, but easily loads into a vehicle, is the best choice. This should help minimize odors that might contaminate the garment fibers. A lot of hunters like to put a pine branch in their tote to keep clothes smelling fresh and piney (and not like plastic).

According to recent reports, in addition to hunting clothing, hunters should also clean their other gear. Backpacks and boots absorb the scents around them. So, store these and other hunting items in areas that aren’t stinky. Use a dedicated storage bin for this gear, too.

The day of the hunt, take a shower with shampoos and soaps that are designed to reduce human odor without adding artificial scents. This should help neutralize some (but not all) of the existing surface scent on your hair and skin.

Brush your teeth, but not with a super-smelly toothpaste. Instead, use something with a natural scent, or no scent at all. Then, eat an apple to help further mitigate scent that might originate from the mouth and throat. Avoid strong-smelling drinks and foods, such as coffee or spicy grub which lead to bad breath.

A lot of hunters use ozone in the field (like Ozonics), but it’s also applicable for treating hunting clothing. Some products are designed to work in conjunction with boxes to clean clothing and remove unwanted scent.

In a recent development, used improperly, Ozone can destroy clothing. So Wildgame innovations recently introduced a ZeroTrace tote and device that is designed to treat gear without destroying it.

Read Next: Does Ozonics Actually Work? Here’s What 5 Independent, Diehard Deer Hunters Say After Field Testing.

To minimize unwanted scent particles from making it onto your hunting clothes, consider dressing once in the field. This keeps away scent from handling pets, visiting gas stations, or other stops between home and the hunt. Getting dressed in the field during a cold or rainy day can be a hassle, but it’s worth it.

Rubber boots can contain some scent, but they only achieve this if kept uncontaminated from foreign scents. Don’t wear your deer hunting boots around town where they might pick up unwanted odors.

Read Next: Best Rubber Hunting Boots.

According to recent reports, hunters have many reasons for field wipes. But in terms of scent control, wiping off sweat with a field wipe will certainly help. Just make sure the version you use is scent-free.

Sources indicate that even better than wiping away sweat, is to not break a sweat at all. Sweat just adds an entire fresh upcoming layer of scent. In the field, do everything possible to prevent or reduce sweating. Wait to put on your coat until you get to your stand.. Walk slowly. Remain in the shade. Take more time to get settled in the treestand.

In a recent development, perhaps the most crucial aspect of scent control is managing the direction that your scent travels. This means choosing good entry and exit routes, and ensuring your wind doesn’t carry over into areas that deer frequent (especially bedding areas and core feeding areas).

Recent findings suggest that those who hope to minimize scent even further should deploy hunting blinds that are completely enclosed. Those which have completely sealed doors and windows can hold most, if not all, scent within the blind. Keeping windows closed until it’s  time to shoot is an excellent way to bottle up scent.

Recent findings suggest that some hunters might cleverly use wind blockers, which are land features that keep deer from getting downwind. Examples include hunting along the edge of a bluff, river, hinge-cut, or lake. Similarly, you can make a mock scrapes on either side of your scent cone, which might stop a buck just long enough before he gets downwind of you.

In a recent development, the rising and falling thermals can be helpful or a huge pain in the butt. When used wisely, and with the right stand locations, thermals will carry scent up and away from deer. For example, hunting up high on a ridge when morning thermals carry scent upward makes it very difficult for deer to smell hunters. Likewise, hunting down low in a bottom when afternoon thermals carry scent downward can achieve the same result.

Industry observers note that remember, no matter how far you take scent control strategies, deer will eventually smell you. It’s important to take all precautions, and implement each step outlined above. Ultimately, careful stand selection that puts the wind in your favor will be the most important step for not getting busted.

Industry observers note that but don’t get discouraged when the inevitable happens. Just keep hunting. After all, you can’t really beat a deer’s nose, and it wouldn’t be fun if we won every time anyway.

‘No Dad, This Is Your Deer.’ Hunter Gets a Second Chance at a 200-Inch Blackpowder Buck

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During Virginia’s muzzleloader season last year, Mike Shifflett got a chance at a giant buck.

It has been revealed that “I was worried I might have hit him,” Shifflett tells Outdoor Life. “But we looked hard and found no evidence he was hit. I sat in a blind later looking for him and eventually spotted him on trail cameras and he was fine. I completely missed him.”.

It has been revealed that virginia had a very harsh winter last year, indicates the 50-year-old farm manager from Crozet, and he was concerned the buck wouldn’t survive. But he started seeing the whitetail again on trail cameras — then found its sheds.

Sources indicate that “I’m sure glad I missed him, because when I started getting trail camera photos of him this summer, his rack had just exploded. His antlers had added at least 30 inches.”.

Shifflett monitored the buck through summer and early autumn on trail cameras in the rolling green hills of northern Virginia. He concluded the deer was very much a loner.

Sources indicate that “He wasn’t aggressive at all,” Shifflett explained. “He completely avoided other bucks. If there was another buck in a field edge I hunted, he’d never come out.”.

Industry observers note that he started hunting the deer during this blackpowder season, which opened Oct. 31 and is Shifflett’s favorite time to chase whitetails.

He got trail camera photos of the buck and saw him once, far away at dusk.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 6, Shifflett waited for his 16-year-old daughter, Chloe, to get home from school, then they rushed to their blind. The hardsided redneck sat  on a field edge near the top of a mountain, with deer trails feeding into the field.

A little after 5 p.m., the buck stepped out at 200 yards. There were some does in the field, and he began working toward them.

It has been revealed that “He worked a scrape and kept walking a few steps at a time toward the does. He was locked on those does, but it took him at least 15 minutes to get to them.

Then the buck, now at 90 yards, started pushing one doe around.

“He was in range and I offered my gun to my daughter to shoot him, but she noted ‘No Dad, this is your deer.’”.

Shifflett raised his scoped .50-cal T/C and fired.

“The air filled with smoke when I shot, and when it cleared the buck had its tail up, and went into the woods. It was surreal, like he wasn’t hit at all.”.

But Chloe had filmed her dad shooting the buck, and the video demonstrated the deer mule kick at the shot.

“But I still didn’t like the way the deer acted as it left the field and into the woods,” states Shifflett.

The two quietly climbed out of the blind and left, planning to return the next morning to track the buck. They returned early the following day with Shifflett’s wife, his son, and a few other helpers.

Recent findings suggest that the search party didn’t initially locate much of a blood trail. But 40 yards into the woods the blood became easy to see. Soon they found the buck dead about 100 yards from the hit site. Shifflet’s bullet had passed through both lungs.

“There was a respectful, silent reverence among us — almost like being in a church.”.

Once they got the buck home, Shifflett and his buddies measured its rack.

“I’m no trophy hunter, and when we started scoring him at home I realized it was a really big buck,” he says. “I had entered a local big buck contest earlier this year and they scored my deer at 194 inches. It’s leading the contest with a $1,000 gift card as top prize.”.

Recent findings suggest that he got in touch with Virginia Buckmasters scorer Tyler Turner, who measured the 16-point whitetail slightly bigger (Buckmasters has a different scoring system than some traditional record keeping organizations, including Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young). His spread was 19.6 inches and taped out at 202 ⅛ inches.

Sources indicate that “Tyler notes it’s the biggest Virginia buck in their ‘Regular Deer’ category that’s ever been taken by bow, blackpowder, or gun. He also told me it’s the ninth largest Buckmasters deer in that rack category nationwide.”.

Industry observers note that it’s been a whirlwind of congratulations since news of his great buck spread. But one thing he says he’ll always remember is when he and his family walked up to the buck that morning.

“When we found him, everyone became real quiet,” he notes. “There was a respectful, silent reverence among us – almost like being in a church.”.
