📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

Recent findings suggest that with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the massive ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

In a recent development, it’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

In a recent development, beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

Sources indicate that there are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern Latest Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

It has been revealed that spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the Upcoming Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Recent findings suggest that why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

According to recent reports, perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

Sources indicate that on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries promptly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

In a recent development, for most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

Not everyone wants to wear techy wraparound sunglasses in town. Thankfully, Smith’s stylish (but still durable and polarized) pair offers the best of both worlds. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which rapidly became his true passion.

Sources indicate that jun once said that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

In a recent development, I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee says that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

Recent findings suggest that jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly released Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

Sources indicate that that was Jun—a man with an unbelievably substantial heart who was always looking for a way to help and who highlighted up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Sources indicate that jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

Climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the single road in Denali National Park winds through the heart of the park and ends in the remote historic mining town of Kantishna. Hikers and cyclists are now able to cross the newly completed Pretty Rocks Bridge, and full public park bus service is set to resume in 2027. (Photo: Pursuit).

It has been revealed that “Bear! On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra. On a steep slope covered with birch trees, pops of autumn amber and rust scattered against green spruce trees, I can make out a moving boulder—then I spot its golden blonde fur. Olivia Juarez, general manager of Denali Backcountry Lodge, tells me it’s the signature coat of Denali grizzlies. Juarez is driving three of us, including her dog, on the entire 92-mile nearly unpaved stretch of the Denali Park Road, which feels precarious at times due to two-thirds of it being only one lane. But the speed limit is 35 mph, and we are the only ones on it.

For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide. But in time for the 2027 summer season, access to the full 92 miles will reopen, allowing visitors to explore the depths of Denali’s backcountry once again.

Recent findings suggest that juarez slows the van to a stop, and we pass around binoculars. The grizzly is far in the distance, but it’s what surrounds it in every direction that catches my breath: striking volcanic cliffs in a kaleidoscope of earthy hues and gravelly, braided glacial streams stretching across an endless expanse of wild. It’s only us on the road, and this grizzly out yonder, for as far as we can see. And out there, somewhere hidden under a cloak of clouds, is Denali, or The Great One, as the peak’s traditional name translates from the Koyukon Athabascan language.

According to recent reports, on September 2, 2026, the long-awaited Pretty Rocks Bridge in Denali National Park was completed, an architectural marvel that bypasses the still-active landslide. At 475 feet long and 24 feet wide, the steel single-span truss bridge is just wide enough for a park bus to drive through.

This $230 million federal project includes 23 underground thermosiphons—a passive cooling technology that pulls heat out of the earth to keep the permafrost frozen year-round. Pedestrians and cyclists are right now permitted to cross, with full bus and vehicle service scheduled to resume in 2027.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent the last four nights at Denali Backcountry Lodge, a remote all-inclusive outpost that sits at the end of the road. I flew in via a 45-mile helicopter ride, the only way guests can reach the property since the landslide. The lodge is the farthest place you can stay and still be in the park. We spent our days hiking through the spongy tundra, exploring the history of the Kantishna mining camp, and kayaking Wonder Lake with Denali in the background, a coveted sight since it was photographed by Ansel Adams on a rare cloudless day in 1947.

Sources indicate that since the road closure, no one other than guests staying at the three remote wilderness lodges has been able to visit these iconic areas of the park. While Denali Backcountry Lodge offers a chance to truly settle into the wild, all the excitement is found along the road. That is, nearly all our wildlife sightings (except for a grizzly sitting atop its moose kill spotted in the distance on one of our guided hikes) happened on a drive: a trio of caribou running, a moose moving through the willow marshes, a porcupine waddling across the road, a bear cub prancing out from the shrubs.

Starting in 2027, visitors will finally be able to reach the end of the road again on a Denali park bus. Guests staying at Denali Backcountry Lodge will arrive and depart via a private bus next year, and their Creekside Cabins guests will take a private bus in and fly out on a single-engine bush plane. Day guests will be able to reach the end of the road and book a guided experience at Denali Backcountry Lodge.

More travelers returning to Denali’s backcountry means there’s more opportunity to transform them into stewards of this land. “Visiting a place like this is life-changing for people,” says Alexa Donahe, vice president and general manager of Pursuit’s Alaska Collection, which includes Denali Backcountry Lodge. “Day traffic allows for more people who don’t have the time or resources to have an immersive backcountry experience like this and to experience the depths of the wilderness for a day.”.

It has been revealed that even with more visitors coming in by bus, it will still feel remote, states Donahe. There will be strict park (and lodge) restrictions to preserve the landscape and wildlife. For comparison, more than 4 million people visit 2.2-million-acre Yellowstone yearly, with easy road access for private cars. Only 500,000 people visit Denali each year, but at 6 million acres, the park is the size of Vermont.

Sure, there are more people gathering at the park entrance, where you’ll find a visitor center and the famous Denali sled dogs, but once you reach the dirt road, it feels as remote as ever.

According to recent reports, only about 30 percent of visitors to Denali National Park and Preserve get a completely clear view of the peak. An even smaller subset—fewer than ten percent—experience a completely cloud-free, base-to-summit view. Visitors who stay multiple days (such as four days in Kantishna) see the mountain at much higher rates, around 85 percent. Because the massive 20,310-foot peak creates its own local weather system, heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the summit, especially during the summer tourism season.

According to recent reports, one morning at breakfast, a group of Natural Habitat guests wait out bad weather to depart. Their expedition leader Samantha Strauss shares with me her thoughts on the fully opened Denali. “For every person who comes out and sees this place, that’s one more person that cares about public lands. Especially right now, public lands are not promised to us,” she says. “Even if that means I have less square mileage allotted just to myself, even if that means I have to share this space with more people, it is a conservation win because it helps people create a connection to the landscape and have a stake in its future.”.

I flew over Denali National Park in a helicopter and left on the Denali Park Road, just days after the Pretty Rocks Bridge bypassing the landslide was completed. Both ways gave me different perspectives on this vast expanse of raw wilderness.

While it was thrilling to soar over glaciers and peaks, it was seeing Denali from the ground, my eyes scanning the landscape for wildlife, moving through the changing early autumn hues, feeling the rush of brisk air as I rolled my window down to take a photo, that made me feel I was a part of it. The road is the center line of this wilderness, and it’s not only the best way to see Denali’s untamed backcountry and wildlife, but to feel its beating heart.

#124965. Latest Update: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2700 w)

Latest Update: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

It has been revealed that located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

In a recent development, posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

According to recent reports, when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

Recent findings suggest that when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he indicates. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

Sources indicate that “The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Recent findings suggest that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that “Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Recent findings suggest that mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

According to recent reports, in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees states. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

Recent findings suggest that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza claims. “The people remarked, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza indicates, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

Sources indicate that while the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

Industry observers note that while sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

According to recent reports, glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Recent findings suggest that of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

It has been revealed that since the collapse of the glacier, a latest group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

Sources indicate that in 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he claims. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I noted, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Recent findings suggest that inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque notes, “but mountain sports have not.”.

Sources indicate that while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he notes. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an vital mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he notes.

It has been revealed that through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily remarked yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he claims.

#124964. Tech Report: How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1517 w)

Tech Report: How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm.
  • It has been revealed that but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important.
  • Sources indicate that but, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

It has been revealed that but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

Sources indicate that but, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

In a recent development, scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s important to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

Recent findings suggest that before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

In a recent development, loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin indicates. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney claims. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

When descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

It has been revealed that with your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

Industry observers note that keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

It has been revealed that you might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”.

It has been revealed that “It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin says. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”.

Recent findings suggest that it comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

In a recent development, rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

And before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney says. “You can just sort of ride it.”.

Recent findings suggest that on a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

According to recent reports, when surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

On particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

“I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin claims. “I never feel like I have that much control.”.

According to recent reports, martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

According to recent reports, if you’re shouldering a particularly substantial pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

It has been revealed that but if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.

#124963. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4453 w)
📖 Baca

How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

These nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

In a recent development, ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

It has been revealed that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

According to recent reports, issues with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Industry observers note that firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “proposal falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

According to recent reports, what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

According to recent reports, if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

The boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

For maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

Industry observers note that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

It has been revealed that have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

It has been revealed that if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

It has been revealed that sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

Industry observers note that the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

Sources indicate that the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

The quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

If those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

The lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

In a recent development, now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

According to recent reports, if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

If you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Sources indicate that even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Sources indicate that besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

Industry observers note that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done swiftly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

According to recent reports, technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a substantial, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

According to recent reports, there are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

In a recent development, lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is vital.

It has been revealed that lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that but, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the problem being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

Industry observers note that if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

But what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

Recent findings suggest that while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a newly introduced stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

But what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is crucial. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

In a recent development, lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

According to recent reports, if the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

Sources indicate that if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

However, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

Speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

It has been revealed that I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Industry observers note that once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

Sources indicate that see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.
