Latest Update: The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes.
  • In a recent development, even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside.
  • Recent findings suggest that the root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes. But athletes of all levels can suffer from them.

In a recent development, even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside. The stronger a skier you are, the harder you can push your quads on the mountain, which means “you can find a way to make them sore, no matter your skiing level,” he explained.

Recent findings suggest that the root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout. When you intensely and repeatedly load your quads, you create microscopic tears in the muscle fibers. That damage may sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: it’s one of the triggers that tells your body to strengthen that muscle, Spencer said.

Still, the side effects can be unpleasant. As with any bodily injury, the microtears trigger swelling, which increases the pain you feel after exercise and causes that sore sensation, Spencer explains. Officially known as delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), this feeling sets in after your workout ends and can peak as late as two to three days after. So if you feel fine boarding the shuttle at the end of a long ski day, but find yourself hobbling to the toilet the next morning, DOMS is probably the culprit.

Industry observers note that the true cure for DOMS is time. “You really just gotta wait for those [microtears] to heal,” Spencer noted. But there’s also something you can do in the interim to ease your pain slightly: quad stretches.

By gently stretching your quads after a hard day on the mountain, you can decrease the intensity of your soreness by flushing out some of the inflammation in your muscles, Spencer remarked. It won’t be a cure-all, but it can help you move and feel better in the short term. Read on for the specific moves Spencer recommends.

You don’t need a ton of quad stretches to find relief. In fact, Spencer indicates two are enough. You’ve probably seen these stretches before, and while, sure, they’re not the most exciting, they are simple and effective.

It has been revealed that optional: Do this stretch in a hot tub. The heat may also help reduce feelings of soreness.

The above stretches can be sufficient to help reduce quad soreness, but if you’re looking for more, Spencer also suggests other recovery methods.

Spend a couple of minutes foam rolling your quads, including the front of your thigh (from the knee all the way up to the hip) and the sides to hit the vastus lateralis (basically where your IT band is). Similar to stretching, foam rolling can bring some relief to the quads by reducing swelling in the area.

Recent findings suggest that another option: hop on a stationary bike and gently cycle your legs for ten to 15 minutes. This easy movement can also reduce soreness by pumping out inflammation from your quads, Spencer noted. Just make sure to keep the resistance and your effort level low. “It’s not meant to be a workout,” he said.

Stretches can ease DOMS in the short term, but if you want to prevent intense soreness altogether, strengthening your quads is the ticket.

Recent findings suggest that “If you just build a little strength going into the season, you’re going to be less sore,” Spencer noted. And you’re also less likely to get injured, he added.

Exercises such as quad sets, wall sits, and really any squat variation like traditional squats, Bulgarian split squats, and single-leg squats can all strengthen the muscle group.

“The thing I hear all the time is the only way to get ready for skiing is by skiing, and that’s a total lie,” Spencer mentioned. There’s a lot you can do both in the off-season and throughout the winter to prime your body for the demands of skiing, he said. In addition to quad-strengthening exercises, he recommends hamstring, glute, and core moves, plus jumping exercises that train your ability to react to the unexpected.

Gary Colliver Was a “Big-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Recent findings suggest that later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a newly introduced route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

It has been revealed that to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Sources indicate that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management initiative for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

Industry observers note that “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher remarked. Although that initial initiative was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

In a recent development, as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular massive wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

#124939. A Basset Hound Revealed Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

A Basset Hound Revealed Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Fresh York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • Industry observers note that the day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Fresh York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

Industry observers note that the day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

It has been revealed that new York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

But time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with plans to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

When the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

In a recent development, finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

“This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch mentioned that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

“It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch said. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so swiftly.”.

It has been revealed that the hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

People with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, stated there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

In a recent development, “In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly says. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

Recent findings suggest that wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he indicates SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody rapidly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

Industry observers note that he says e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Industry observers note that urgency is particularly key in these cases, Cooper says. Research demonstrates that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper says, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

#124937. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2350 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • Recent findings suggest that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • In a recent development, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

Recent findings suggest that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

In a recent development, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

In a recent development, on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and rapidly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

Recent findings suggest that I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

In a recent development, as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

According to recent reports, as excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

According to recent reports, among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in substantial walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

It has been revealed that the first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

It has been revealed that around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we promptly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Recent findings suggest that not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

It has been revealed that 1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#124936. Breaking: Hike of the Week: Explore the Dramatic—and Threatened—Big Bend on This Desert Peak

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Hike of the Week: Explore the Dramatic—and Threatened—Big Bend on This Desert Peak

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S.
  • Nine years later, Big Bend is still beautiful.
  • One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: kellyvandellen/Getty Images).

Industry observers note that the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S. and Mexico, I was amazed not just at how beautiful it was, but how peaceful. The buff and black-streaked limestone walls soared 1,500 feet over the water, the afternoon sun streaming through the gap. The river was running low and slow, trickling over the mud and rocks, no more than knee deep. I rolled up my pant legs and waded into the water, toward that invisible line in the middle of the river that split two countries.

Nine years later, Big Bend is still beautiful. Covering an area bigger than Rhode Island, this stretch of West Texas desert is home to some of the state’s most moving scenery, from river canyons to rocky peaks, with animal and plant life to match. Hikers willing to put in the work on the area’s rugged trails may spot javelinas rooting in the undergrowth or nocturnal, raccoon-like ringtails climbing up the cliffs and trees of the Chisos Mountains; they’ll see prickly pear cactus and ocotillo, a spindly, Seussian shrub equipped with vicious spines, growing wild in the desert flats. (That border, however, may soon be far more concrete. Read on for more on that.).

One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak. At 7,825 feet, Emory is the highest point in Big Bend and the Chisos, and enjoys commanding views of the terrain for miles around. Getting there, however, takes some muscle: The rough, 9.7-mile hike to the top ascends singletrack and rock stairs through oak, piñon, and juniper forest before ending with a final, dramatic scramble to the peak’s exposed summit. November, when summer’s broiling temperatures finally cool down, is an ideal time to hike it. (Note: There is no water at all along the Emory Peak Trail, and the NPS suggests hikers carry at least one liter per person per hour.).

The round trip takes about 6 to 8 hours, and you’ll want to leave some time to relax afterward. Santa Elena Canyon’s picnic area is an ideal spot for an early dinner, and cap off the night at the park’s free riverside hot springs. (Due to recent flood damage, reaching both of these highlights is presently harder than usual. The paved road between Cottonwood Campground and Santa Elena is closed at the time of writing; drivers with a true 4-wheel drive vehicle and high clearance can get there on Old Maverick Road. Due to another closure, getting to the hot springs requires a 4-mile round-trip, relatively flat hike along a gravel road. Consider it part of the adventure.).

In a recent development, starting at the Chisos Basin Visitors Center, take the Laguna Meadows trail for about a third of a mile to a fork, where you’ll hang a left on the Pinnacles Trail. Follow it as it steadily climbs, traversing desert flats and rocky slopes with the sheer top of Emory looming in the background. After another 3.4 miles, the trail reaches a saddle below the top of the peak. Continue on the Emory Peak Trail for another 1.5 miles, then tackle a final, somewhat exposed 30-foot scramble to the top of the mountain and 360-degree views of the park below. Retrace your steps to the trailhead, or break up the hike by reserving one of the Pinnacles campsites ahead of your trip.

In an 8-1 decision on November 9, the Supreme Court approved a request by the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall through Significant Bend, ruling against plaintiffs who had argued that the barrier would decimate rare plant species and cut off migratory routes for animals, and that it risked damaging ancient rock art and Native heritage sites. In Santa Elena Canyon itself, the Department of Homeland Security plans to install vehicle barriers and surveillance infrastructure and clear patrol roads through the area. Conservation groups and state officials like Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa say they’ll continue to push to end construction in the park.

#124935. Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1011 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).
  • For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.
  • In interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).

For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.

In interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route. Atop his list of concerns, however, was the deadly Khumbu Icefall, the site of avalanches and dangerous crumbling seracs. Every spring, Sherpa porters and guides must make dozens of trips through the crumbling glacier to ferry food, tents, and oxygen to higher camps.

It has been revealed that “If you run 20 trips on Everest over the next 20 years and hire 15 to 20 Sherpas each year, you’re putting a lot of people’s lives in danger,” Ballinger told Outside in a 2023 interview. “We don’t feel that we can run an ethical expedition from the south side.”.

Ballinger’s tech giant, Alpenglow Expeditions, led a handful of trips to Everest’s south side in the aughts. But starting in 2014, Alpenglow exclusively led Everest trips from the mountain’s northern side in Tibet, which is controlled by China.

In a recent development, now, Ballinger is taking steps to return to Everest’s southern side. In a recent interview, he told Outside that his three-year strategy for Alpenglow is to lead trips up Everest from both Tibet and Nepal concurrently.

“Even though we still think the north side of Everest is better for our clients, we are considering the south side as a backup,” Ballinger remarked. “And ultimately, we hope to be able to run trips on both sides of the mountain, provided we get the approvals that we expect.”.

Returning to Nepal gives Alpenglow a backup plan in case China closes the peak to climbers, Ballinger remarked.

Climbers tackling Everest from the northern side of the China-Nepal border enjoy a few advantages, namely smaller crowds and a Base Camp accessible by vehicles. But the Chinese government’s repeated decision to close Everest with little warning has stymied expedition leaders. In 2008, China closed Everest just weeks before the climbing season to allow the Olympic torch relay to ascend the peak.

Industry observers note that since 2016, China has shuttered Everest five additional times. It closed the peak in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic, and kept Everest off-limits through the 2023 season. Ballinger returned the following year with an expedition to the top.

“We had incredible seasons on Everest in 2024 and 2025, some of the best of my life,” Ballinger said. “It was uncrowded, we had great support from the Chinese, and it was totally open.”.

In 2026, Ballinger and other guides were preparing for another successful season on Everest’s north side when China abruptly canceled the season in early March. The decision came painfully late in the season. Expedition operators had already promised paychecks to guides and mountain workers. And climbers usually arrive at Base Camps in China and Nepal in mid-April.

Industry observers note that “We took the financial losses and did the right thing,” Ballinger said. “We paid our Sherpas and our guides and our workers who waited until the end. We ate that cost.”.

It has been revealed that ballinger said he then gave his climbing clients refunds or deferrals to the 2027 season. One-third accepted deferrals to 2027, while two-thirds booked with other outfitters in Nepal in 2026, he said. Alpenglow helped its clients find expeditions to join on Everest’s south side for the 2026 season.

Sources indicate that “Financially it’s not easy,” Ballinger said. “It definitely sucks, but we want the best for our clients.”.

Operating in both Nepal and Tibet, however, would allow Alpenglow to shift clients from one side of the peak to the other in the instance of a closure.

Industry observers note that “Between 2007 and this year—that’s 20 seasons—we’ve had to cancel six times,” he noted. “In those years there’s a lot of stress.”.

Ballinger cited the rapid introduction of cargo-carrying drones on Everest’s south side as another reason for his decision to return. In 2026, a company called Airlift Technologies began ferrying gear and supplies from Base Camp at 17,500 feet over the Khumbu Icefall up to Camp I at 19,900 feet via heavy-duty cargo drones.

Alpenglow’s lead guide, Esteban “Topo” Mena, spent time at the Nepali Base Camp in 2026 to watch the business grow.

“We sent Topo to check out the scene and see if he thought the experimentation that’s going on with drone technology had a meaningful impact,” Ballinger noted. “We think we can replace all of our Sherpa carries through the Khumbu Icefall with drones.”.

It has been revealed that each drone delivery to Camp I eliminates a human trip through the Khumbu Icefall. In 2026, several Everest outfitters relied heavily on Airlift Technologies’ drone service to transport gear above Base Camp.

The drone business grew out of two seasons of testing. Starting in 2024, Nepali drone companies began completing test flights of heavy-duty cargo drones amid the thin air at Everest Base Camp. In 2025, drone pilots successfully flew an oxygen canister and bags of gear from Base Camp to Camp I, proving the potential for a drone business.

The drone business is not without its problems. In 2026, the Nepali government grounded Airlift Technologies’ drones for four days without explanation.

Recent findings suggest that piloting a cargo drone over the Khumbu Icefall requires skill and technological innovation. One pilot at Base Camp controls the drone at takeoff. But when the craft reaches a specific elevation, a second pilot at Camp I takes over control, navigating the craft past towers of ice and sheer rock walls to land it on the upper flanks of the Khumbu Glacier.

It has been revealed that “We see it as a really exciting change,” Ballinger remarked. “We’ve been talking for years now about what would allow the icefall to become manageable in the long term. We think drones are a stepping stone in that direction.”.

#124930. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1358 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks.
  • Recent findings suggest that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good tech giant.”.

Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Currently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she indicates of her massive three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Recent findings suggest that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

According to recent reports, I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

In a recent development, when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It has been revealed that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we rapidly got all our stuff together.

Industry observers note that we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

Sources indicate that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Sources indicate that very promptly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

Sources indicate that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

In a recent development, then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

It has been revealed that so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a latest belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he said it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

It has been revealed that I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

Industry observers note that it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a major light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

According to recent reports, to really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

According to recent reports, lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to New York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#124926. 6 Underrated Mountain Towns to Visit This Winter

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2209 w)

6 Underrated Mountain Towns to Visit This Winter

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These are the mountain towns that dominate our winter daydreams.
  • I cover mountain towns for Outside, and every year I start plotting out my own winter getaways right about now.
  • It has been revealed that A couple of these towns are my longtime favorites, while others are still on my “must-go” list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know the major names. Jackson, Wyoming. Stowe, Vermont. Telluride, Colorado. These are the mountain towns that dominate our winter daydreams. The famous ski towns that make us consider taking a sabbatical, buying a van, and living the Aspen Extreme dream for three months in the heart of winter. But there are other winter adventure spots that deserve the spotlight.

I cover mountain towns for Outside, and every year I start plotting out my own winter getaways right about now. Sure, I enjoy hitting up established destinations like Park City as much as the next skier, but the towns on this list get me excited because they fly under the radar. They don’t receive a ton of hype, but they have access to amazing powder stashes, lengthy trail systems, and resort lines that are far shorter than their better-known counterparts’.

It has been revealed that A couple of these towns are my longtime favorites, while others are still on my “must-go” list. Here are six often overlooked winter mountain towns that you need to visit once the snow starts to gather.

A legitimate winter town in the South? Yes indeed. Boone is a vibrant college town that grows when Appalachian State’s roughly 20,000 students are in session. It has all of the hallmarks of a fun-loving mountain town, with plenty of dive bars and burrito joints to keep you satiated. But it also sits in North Carolina’s High Country, surrounded by 5,000- and 6,000-foot mountains, which get some of the heaviest snowfalls in the region. There are three ski resorts within 30 minutes of downtown and some of the most consistent cross-country skiing in the South on a series of 6,000-foot peaks near the Tennessee border.

In a recent development, winter Adventures: You have three downhill resorts to choose from, but Beech Mountain Resort is the highest ski resort in eastern North America, with a summit elevation of 5,506 feet. It also has a bar, the 5506′ Skybar, at the top of the mountain and its own brewery in the base village. As for the terrain, the mountain has 95 acres and just over 800 feet of drop, so you’ll need to do laps to get in your vert. But the terrain park gets better every year, and skiers can usually count on about 80 inches of snow every winter. Full-day adult lift tickets start at $57 on weekdays.

But the best winter adventure near Boone is cross-country skiing Roan Mountain, a high ridge that tops out at 6,285 feet, gets heavy snowfall, and has a variety of terrain to ski, from high-elevation grassy balds to singletrack through rhododendron tunnels. The only catch is you’ll need to bring your own skis, as rentals are scarce in the South. Start at Carver’s Gap and head up the gated Forest Service road, which climbs gradually for about two miles to the Rhododendron Gardens. You’ll get long-range views in both directions and the option to hop onto more challenging trails that branch off the road.

Duluth is a longtime shipping and industrial city at the western tip of Lake Superior that has found upcoming life as an adventure hub, with a world-class mountain bike trail system traversing the hills on the edge of downtown. But the city’s location in northern Minnesota means winter hits the city hard. Duluth gets about 86 inches of lake-effect snow each winter, and that snow sticks around because high temperatures stay below freezing on more than 100 days a year. The constant cold temps are ideal for ice climbing, and the consistent snow and cornucopia of mountain bike trails mean Duluth becomes a fat-biking and cross-country ski mecca during winter.

Sources indicate that need more reasons to visit? How about downhill skiing at nearby Spirit Mountain, which has 175 acres of terrain with 700 feet of vertical drop.

In a recent development, winter Adventures: Northern Minnesota has a legitimate ski culture, and Spirit Mountain has some of the best blue cruisers in the Midwest, many of which have long-range views of downtown Duluth and Lake Superior. The mountain also has two terrain parks, one for beginners looking to progress and one for shredders looking to send it. There’s a welcoming uphill policy for anyone who wants to earn their turns on touring gear, too. Adult tickets start at $83.

But Duluth is a bike town, and when the snow falls that means it’s time to roll out the fat tires. Many sections of the Duluth Traverse, an epic 40-mile-long route that runs from one side of the city to the other, are groomed for fat bikes in the winter. The machine-built trails in Mission Creek, with their berms and rollers, are particularly fun with a layer of packed snow. Local outfitter Day Tripper offers guided fat-bike tours and rentals.

New England got hammered with snow last winter, with the highest elevations in the mountains getting more than 200 inches of snow, and the tiny town of Jackson was poised to make the most of it. This picture-perfect village, which comes complete with a general store and covered bridge, sits on the edge of White Mountain National Forest with fast access to downhill skiing at Black Mountain and roughly 90 miles of cross-country ski trails scattered throughout the valley.

Sources indicate that jackson doesn’t have the cachet of some other ski towns in Fresh England, but American ski culture got an early boost here when Black Mountain opened in 1935, making it one of the first lift operations in the country. And that culture is still thriving. Case in point: check out Friday Night Lights, a weekly uphill party where skiers put on headlamps and ski to the top of the mountain en masse.

Industry observers note that winter Adventures: The Jackson Ski Touring Foundation grooms and maintains about 150 kilometers of trails, all surrounding a touring center with rentals and lessons. The trails traverse the community throughout three consecutive river valleys over 60 square miles. You’ll get views of Mount Washington from open meadows, tight singletrack through woods, and even the chance to hit trailside restaurants in certain spots. Day passes start at $29.

No trip to Jackson is complete without some laps at Black Mountain, a proudly independent ski resort with 140 acres of glades, narrow groomers, and nonexistent lift lines. You’ll get 1,100 feet of vertical drop, with the steepest terrain at the summit, and a lively pub (the Shovel Handle Pub) at the base of the mountain for après-ski activities. Adult lift tickets start at $49.

Sources indicate that the San Juan Mountains are home to some of Colorado’s most iconic mountain towns and most well-regarded ski slopes, but most skiers don’t explore the region beyond Telluride and Silverton. Dig deeper into the mountains of southwest Colorado and you’ll find tiny Pagosa Springs, which sits on the banks of the San Juan River. The hamlet is best known for its geothermal springs, but the mountains surrounding this hot-water hub are even more enticing. Pagosa Springs is 23 miles from Wolf Creek Ski Area, which is known as one of the snowiest mountains in Colorado, pulling down an average of 430 inches of snow every winter.

Want more variety? Summer waterfalls turn into ice-climbing playgrounds when the temperature drops, and the local Nordic club grooms more than 50 kilometers of skate and classic ski trails near town.

Winter Adventures: Forget the champagne huts and concierge service you find at many ski resorts these days. Wolf Creek is a no-frills operation that’s all about the snow and the terrain, with 430 inches of annual snowfall that blanket wide groomers and steep trees. OK, a lot of trees. Wolf Creek has a significant amount of expert terrain, which plays out in a series of steep bowls at the top of the resort and seemingly endless glades all over the mountain. And you won’t have to take out a loan to fund this trip; full-day adult lift tickets at Wolf Creek are right at $110.

Industry observers note that the 50 kilometers of cross-country ski trails begin in town, with a mile-long loop inside the town park that’s perfect for beginners. But this is a great chance to dip a toe into fat biking. There’s an 8.5-mile loop that’s groomed for fat bikes when snow allows, winding through a ponderosa pine forest. Pagosa Mountain Sport rents cross-country skis and fat bikes.

Park City, Salt Lake City…these are the ski towns that get the press, but Ogden? Ogden doesn’t typically make the list. But it should. This historic city, which was the first permanent settlement by people of European descent in the state of Utah, sits between the Great Salt Lake and the Wasatch Mountains, just 40 minutes north of Salt Lake City, but seemingly a world apart. Downtown Ogden is anchored by 25th Street, a historic main street with upscale Wild West charm, while three ski resorts known for deep powder are less than 30 minutes away. Powder Mountain anchors the trio, with more than 8,000 acres of terrain, but Snowbasin is continually ranked one of the best ski resorts in the country by Ski magazine and the smaller Nordic Valley has a local-hill vibe complete with night skiing. Bonus: You don’t have to fight Salt Lake City’s notorious canyon traffic to make your turns.

Recent findings suggest that winter Adventures: You’re here to ski, so get after it at Powder Mountain, the largest ski resort in the Lower 48. Powder has 2,800 acres of lift-served terrain with more than 2,000 feet of vertical drop, but the real gem here is Powder’s sidecountry. Head through the Powder Country or Woody’s World entrance gates from the lift-served side of the mountain and you’ll have 1,200 acres of ungroomed, off-piste action at your ski tips. The best part? A shuttle bus picks you up at the bottom of your line and takes you back to the front of the mountain, so there’s no boot-packing involved. Adult lift tickets start at $99.

You might also want to try your hand at sledding AKA snowmobiling while you’re in Ogden. The Monte Cristo area, east of the Ogden Valley, has some of the best snowmobile terrain in the state, including a 63-mile groomed loop that’s perfect for beginners and has long-range views of the Ogden Valley. Club Rec North offers tours and rentals next to the trailhead. Tours with rentals start at $229.

This former gold-mining post in the North Cascades really leans into its historic roots, with a downtown that’s lined with Old West-style false fronts and wooden boardwalks. And that western heritage is still alive and well. A number of outfitters offer horseback adventures and the annual Ride to Rendezvous, a four-day horse-packing trip complete with a wagon train that rolls into town for Winthrop’s ’49er Days parade. But make no mistake, Winthrop has found new life as a ski town. Well, a skinny-ski town. The Methow Valley surrounding Winthrop has one of the most extensive cross-country trail networks in the country with more than 120 miles of groomed, marked and maintained paths to explore.

Sources indicate that looking for a cozy vibe for the whole family? Take a spin around Winthrop Rink, the town’s outdoor ice-skating rink that serves as the social hub for the season.

In a recent development, winter Adventures: If you’re spending time in Winthrop, then you’re here to ski the Methow Trails. With more than 120 miles of obsessively groomed paths, there is something for everyone in this valley. Want to ski from lodge to lodge? That’s an option. Want a pretty loop around a lake? No problem. Want to spend the day climbing an obscene amount of vertical? They have you covered. The Methow Trails organization runs clinics and camps all season if you want to improve your kick-and-glide form or maybe try your hand at biathlon. Day passes start at $32.

Sources indicate that loup Loup Ski Bowl is a lift-served mountain with 300 acres that’s operated by a nonprofit. There are 10 runs with 1,240 vertical feet of drop. You’ll find beginner trails and expert trails that drop from the top of the mountain and a very welcoming uphill ski culture if you want to earn your turns. And you’ve got to check out the Ski Bowl’s luge course, where you guide an old-school sled down groomed trails. Adult lift tickets start at $80.

Graham Averill is Outside magazine’s national parks columnist. He loves warm-weather adventures, but he gets absolutely giddy when ski season approaches, and writing articles like this helps him initiative his ski trips.

Breaking: Unequipped Hikers Rescued from Winter Storm on Colorado Section of the Continental Divide Trail

  • Located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that snow on the mountains above Rollins Pass, Colorado. (Photo: SWKrullImaging via Getty).

A late fall hike turned into an overnight rescue on the Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail on November 14 when a trio of hikers called for a rescue after encountering severe weather and wintry conditions at 11,600 feet.

Located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet. When hiked in its entirety, it also involves 3,742 feet of elevation gain over the course of 18 miles. Recent day-time temperature highs in the area have hovered between 26 and 37 degrees, while lows were recorded at 5 and 9 degrees with wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

Sources indicate that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR), which responded, noted that the hikers called for help after encountering dangerous trail conditions, significant snow, and navigational struggles. The team dispatched a group of rescuers who rode ATVs up the Rollins Pass Road before dismounting and hiking the remaining distance there. When rescuers made it to the trio, they found the hikers were wet, cold, and tired.

“The subjects had set up camp but lacked appropriate gear, including fire making supplies, to spend the night in the deteriorating weather,” rescue officials wrote. A second rescue team joined the party later in the evening before accompanying the hikers back to the staged ATVs and from there to the trailhead.

In a recent development, although most of Grand County has yet to see significant snow, November can be a deceptive time of the year to hike in Colorado’s high country. Trails may appear accessible, but factors like extreme temperatures, inclement weather and reduced daylight hours can make hiking and camping more treacherous than usual.

The Continental Divide Trail is the highest-elevation long trail in the United States, with its high point at the summit of 14,278-foot Grays Peak. Colorado’s section is the highest on the trail; the USFS estimates that the CDT’s average elevation across the state is 10,000 feet.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • Industry observers note that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

Industry observers note that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Sources indicate that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

According to recent reports, insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

In a recent development, now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Fresh Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Industry observers note that print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Industry observers note that once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.
